maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND REPUBLIC OF KOREA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to table the text in English and French of the trade agreement between Canada and the Republic of Korea and the documents pertaining thereto. The agreement came into force-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND REPUBLIC OF KOREA
speechtext: Order, please. Has the minister leave to table these documents?

maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND REPUBLIC OF KOREA
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND REPUBLIC OF KOREA
speechtext:
The agreement came into force upon signature, which took place in Ottawa on December 20. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and I signed on behalf of Canada. Under the agreement, Canada will accord to imports from Korea the rates of the most favoured nations tariff which are now applied to imports from the United States, Japan and other most favoured nation countries. In return Canadian goods are assured of as favourable tariff treatment by Korea as those from any other country.
There is also an understanding with respect to the access to the Korean market for goods of particular interest to Canada which may be affected by the balance of payments controls applied by Korea. This understanding is in a separate exchange of letters. There are also separate undertakings to deal with possible problems of market disruption which may arise in the future as well as the application by Korea of voluntary restraints on exports to Canada of certain goods for the 12 month period beginning January 1, 1967. These goods are listed in the annex to the correspondence between the Korean embassy in Ottawa and the Department of Finance.
11514	COMMONS
Tributes to the Late Rodger Mitchell
This agreement marks a further step in our program for expanding Canada's trade and economic relations with our neighbours across the Pacific. Canada has supported the accession of Korea to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade which is expected to take place shortly. At the present time trade between Canada and Korea is relatively small. Under this agreement we look forward to a mutually advantageous expansion of this trade. With the signing of this agreement, Canada now has formal trade relations with a total of 104 countries.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF HON. MEMBER FOR SUDBURY

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF HON. MEMBER FOR SUDBURY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my sad duty to announce to the house the passing, since we last sat, of Mr. Rodger Mitchell, our colleague the hon. member for Sudbury. Mr. Mitchell had been ill for some time. He had borne that illness with the quiet courage and uncomplaining spirit that was characteristic of him. Only a week or so before he died I had information that he was making a recovery, which was very unusual in the circumstances, and we hoped that perhaps he would get over this illness. That was not to be.
Hon. members on all sides of the house will, I know, join me in regret at his passing. I think he was one of the most highly regarded and best loved members in the house. He was quiet and sincere in his devotion to duty as a member and also a very dedicated and loyal Canadian. He will be greatly missed, I know, by all hon. members, perhaps by me as much as by any other member because we represented adjoining constituencies in the House of Commons and I have benefited for many, many years by his wise advice and good counsel.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF HON. MEMBER FOR SUDBURY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Rodger Mitchell was one of those members who enjoyed the respect of hon. members in all parts of the house. He did not participate in debates generally, but he gave devotedly to his constituency and to his country. He had a wonderfully friendly disposition and, above all, in recent months when facing a fatal illness, of which he knew, he displayed a courage that was almost unbelievable. I talked with him on the last occasion he was here, and he was still full of hope and optimism. All of us in Her

DEBATES	January 9, 1967
Majesty's loyal opposition wish to extend our sympathy to his loved ones, to the Prime Minister and to the members of the government party.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF HON. MEMBER FOR SUDBURY
speechtext:
The members of the New Democratic Party wish to associate themselves with the tributes which have just been paid to our late colleague Rodger Mitchell. He gave good service to his constituency and to the House of Commons. He was highly regarded and greatly respected by all those who worked with him. Those of us who have been associated with him know what a pleasant travelling companion he was. Despite the fact that he was suffering from ill health, he was one of the most active members of the house, and all of us who worked with him on various occasions came to have a very high regard for him. I am sure that his loss will be felt keenly not only in the house but in the constituency which he so ably represented in parliament.
Members of this party would like to extend to the bereaved family, to the Prime Minister and to Rodger Mitchell's colleagues in the house our deepest sympathy in this sad time of loss.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF HON. MEMBER FOR SUDBURY

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party and personally, I wish to join with the previous speakers to deplore the passing away of a member of this house, Mr. Mitchell. I knew him personally as a fellow member on two delegations. He had a very strong social awareness; he was a very interesting travelling companion and a hard worker.
To his leader and his party, as well as to the members of his family, I wish to extend our party's deepest sympathy.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF HON. MEMBER FOR SUDBURY

This sad event reminds us of life itself and of the frequency with which we have to rise on occasions like this because of the passing of one of our colleagues. speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman's question covered a good deal of ground, and my answer will have to be a little longer than would normally be desirable. I should like to begin by saying that the peaceful demonstration in Toronto to which the right hon. gentleman was obviously referring had nothing whatever to do with the 23033-730
Inquiries of the Ministry Company of Young Canadians, which was not involved. The two volunteers reported in the press as having taken part did so in their personal capacity as citizens of a free country.
When this house approved the establishment of the Company of Young Canadians last summer we knew, I believe, that we were creating an organization which was expected to be characterized by a spirit of innovation, and of zeal in a new and uncharted field of public service. I stated at that time, and I am glad to repeat it, that "this is not only to be a company for young Canadians, but a company of young Canadians, a company in which young Canadians themselves will play a major role in determining the plans, operations and objectives." In this regard, I believe, the company must have a maximum degree of independence as it seeks to channel the idealism of youth into constructive social action.
I believe it is important at this time to make it clear that the original purposes of the company still have the fullest support of the government and, I hope, of the house. I wish to take this opportunity of reaffirming my confidence in the young men and women who are now serving in the company as volunteers, as staff members and as members of the provisional council. Transportation
On clause 1-National transportation policy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, no piece of legislation that will be before the house this year will be of greater importance to the future development of the Atlantic provinces than this bill. I feel certain that the Minister of Transport is well aware of the fears and apprehensions of the people of that area in so far as transportation policy is concerned. We have found in the past 100 years that in so far as transportation policy is concerned everything has been a gamble in the hope of improved conditions in our area in respect of development, a gamble that has almost constantly and continuously proven to be a poor one as far as we have been concerned.
In recent weeks we have seen a certain attitude developing in the province of Quebec with regard to the celebration or lack of celebration of our centennial year in that province. All I can say is that if there is an area of Canada that has less reason to celebrate confederation than the maritime provinces I would like to know what area it is, but certainly it is not the province of Quebec. Our area of Canada has contributed the most and received the least for its contribution in becoming a part of confederation. While we have made this contribution and recognize this fact, we still believe that the move we made in 1867 was the right one. We face our problems, we try to do something about them, and we like to join with Canadians in all parts of this nation in celebrating a wonderful year, one which we hope will lead to 100 years of prosperity for all parts of Canada.
As has been enunciated by the hon. members for Halifax and the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, for those in our port cities there has been a very substantial deterioration each and every year in the degree of business available to those ports because of policies which have been adopted by the Department of Transport and are continuously being implemented with regard to opening up shipping lanes in the province of Quebec and especially to the port of Montreal. I read over the week end an article which appeared in the Montreal Star of January 7. The statistics quoted in that article indicate to a significant degree the reason for the concern expressed by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and the hon. members for Halifax, and the extent of the deterioration in our port business.
In December the Minister of Transport was in our area of Nova Scotia and also in New Brunswick, attending port dinners. In effect he

January 9, 1967
Transportation
told the people in the audiences at those dinners that he was not going to do anything about what was happening in so far as shipping on the St. Lawrence river was concerned and the ice-breaking facilities of his department. As usual, lack of action by the government will cause the economy of the maritime provinces to lag.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I think it is worth while putting the statistics on the record. They refer to ship arrivals at Montreal between January 1 and March 31. In 1960 five ocean-going vessels and two coastal traders tied up at Montreal, or a total of seven ships. The foreign tonnage represented was 14,971 and the domestic tonnage was 2,398. Let us compare these figures with the year 1966. During the six years between 1960 and 1966 the number of ocean-going vessels which tied up in Montreal increased from five to 56, the number of coastal vessels increased from two to 63, and the total increased from seven to 119. The tonnage carried by foreign vessels increased from 14,971 to 214,352, an increase of about 200,000 tons. Domestic tonnage increased from 2,398 to 289,942, or 287,600 tons more than in 1960. If the government does not act there will be no more business at the ports of Halifax and Saint John in the wintertime than in the summertime, and if this situation continues the economy of the Atlantic provinces, especially the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, will greatly deteriorate.
Last night on the television news photographs were shown indicating the greatly decreased shipping at the port of Halifax. Indeed it is shocking to discover the small amount of business at that port at the present time and the great unemployment among stevedores who have to depend on winter employment for their yearly earnings. If the Minister of Transport has his way, this situation will be allowed to continue. We are dealing with a national transportation policy. If this is to be part of that policy, then God help the maritime provinces because the government will do nothing to help them and the Lord is the only one from whom hope may come. We must pray a great deal if we ever hope to get anything because it is quite evident that we will get nothing from the government.
If we were the kind of people who did not believe in contracts that we had signed, once again black bands would be worn in Nova Scotia as they were in 1867 when that province became part of this nation. These are dark days for the people of the maritime provinces so far as the transportation policy is

concerned and in many other fields, as is indicated by the substantial lay-offs which have been taking place in many of our industries.
Not all our problems concern coal. We have problems with steel and problems in just trying to survive. The policies which the government has been putting forward every day do not spell progress for us. Surely we should be able to expect something more from the Minister of Transport who represents a constituency in the Atlantic provinces. He has seen the statistics on the tonnage which our ports are losing. We are told by him that we can expect nothing more than we have received up to date. He sits on his hands and lets the business which for years we expected to come to us go to the province of Quebec, an area which does not wish to take any part in the centennial program because its people are not happy with what they are getting at present. If they are not happy with what they are getting now, let us realize how much sadder we in Nova Scotia should be when every day that this government is in office we get less and less.
This is not the kind of policy which we were led to believe would be established when this government came to office. Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is any question in the mind of any member sitting in this chamber as to the great consequences this bill will have on the entire transportation system of Canada. On reading the bill there can also be no question in anyone's mind as to its complexities. No one qua-relled with the objective that the government had in mind in introducing this bill, that of trying to evolve a transportation system to serve Canada as a whole. I do not think anybody took serious issue with the government over an honest attempt to put the railways in the position where they were self-sustaining rather than financed by government subsidies to such a large extent.
I was impressed with the presentation of the minister on television when he was questioned on this subject. He stated that the taxpayers would be duly concerned about any increase in subsidy above $100 million, and I think he is correct in making that assumption.
My reason for rising today, Mr. Chairman, has to do with the fact that during this entire
Transportation
debate and in the many debates which have preceded it on the subject of transportation constant reference has been made to the vast distances between the eastern and western regions of Canada. We are told about the vast distances covered, the services rendered and the costs involved in covering these vast distances.
The arguments in this connection are very valid indeed, but what we tend to forget are the complexities and problems which arise as a result of similar vast distances between the northern and southern areas of Canada. I think, for example, of the distance between Windsor in Ontario and the port of Churchill in northern Manitoba. The problems relating to the port of Churchill and to the northern areas of Ontario and Manitoba will be dealt with in detail by other hon. members but I wish to take a few moments, if I may, to talk about the particular problems with which we in southern Ontario are faced as a result of our geographic location.
If you were to refer to a map of Canada, Mr. Chairman, I am sure you would realize what a problem we have owing to the fact that we are located so far to the south. As a matter of fact, I believe southern Ontario is almost on the same latitude as the city of New York. As a result of this geographic location the people of southerstern Ontario engaged in industry and in business as well as in various aspects of transportation have for many years felt that they have been working under a tremendous handicap as a result of the regulations previously laid down to govern transportation, especially railway transportation. I am sure the minister is aware of this.
Recently a presentation was made to the transportation committee by the Windsor Chamber of Commerce which, may I point out, spoke with the complete support of the various chambers of commerce and municipalities in that area. When the presentation was made to the transportation committee in connection with this particular problem, I am certain I am being fair when I say that the minister expressed sympathy with their view and also expressed the hope that when this bill in its amended form was once more presented to the house certain areas would be granted the relief which they sought.
In talking with the various interests concerned with transportation there appears to be a general feeling that the amendments which have been made in the revised version of the bill will not provide an avenue for

granting the relief which was so earnestly sought. There is no doubt that the people of southwestern Ontario will find it increasingly hard to compete with other areas of Canada if the present system of railway rate allocation is incorporated in this revised bill.

You will recall, Mr. Chairman,-it has been pointed out by many briefs from that area and also in this house by myself and other members-that because of our geographic location we are subjected to one type of railway charge in moving goods eastward and to another type in moving goods westward. This means that in moving goods from Windsor to the harbour of Halifax the rate on first-class goods on a pound per mile basis is roughly twice as great as the rate from Montreal to Halifax. This appears to be fair and justifiable because the distance from Windsor to Halifax is almost twice as great as from Montreal to Halifax. But when we move goods west we find that this is not the system followed. When goods are moved, for example, from Windsor to Winnipeg, though Windsor is 600 miles closer to Winnipeg than is Montreal the rate from Windsor is almost identical with the rate from Montreal. We maintain that this does not appear to be fair. Because of our location, when we wish to move goods westward we are charged on the basis that all goods moving out of our area have to move east, almost to Toronto, before they can move west. Therefore we are subjected to a double rate.
That this sort of thing will have a tremendous impact on our area, if incorporated in the new bill, is borne out by the fact that when the area in question in southwestern Ontario was made a designated area with special tax concessions, over the period of the next two or three ensuing years there was a tremendous influx of almost every type of industry. The industries ranged from the very large to very small subcontractors. This influx had the effect of bringing a vitality to the area which had been sadly lacking for some time.
Those who have studied this subject are convinced that if we are subjected to an excessive charge in moving our goods westward the effect will be to slow down the influx of new industry, to curtail the expansion of industries already in the area, and generally to apply the brakes to growth. As a matter of fact this has already started. Some industries have thought that under this bill the relief that is necessary will perhaps not be obtained.

It is true that large industries, because of their political power and because of the tremendous tonnage they move, are able to negotiate special rates with the railways. One would expect this to be so. Perhaps in the new bill as envisaged by the minister more scope will be given for this type of negotiation. A tremendous number of small industries will not derive benefit from this type of negotiation, first, because the volume of goods they ship does not merit such negotiation and, second, because they have not the necessary pressure to enforce their wishes in negotiating with a body as large as a railway company. It is true that small industries will not be able to negotiate in this way but the aggregate tonnage of the production they ship is tremendous. Were such industries to act as one body they could perhaps obtain the rates now enjoyed by some of the major industries.
The minister has said that under the terms of this bill special consideration will be given to captive markets. I know the minister will dispute with me, perhaps with justification, any allegation that the area I represent in southwestern Ontario is a captive market. He will say, I am sure, that not only have we access to two railways, to four if you count United States lines, but that we have access to trucking and water transportation companies. If this were the entire story the minister would be absolutely correct in his assertion. But from the point of view of businessmen I am sure the minister will agree with me that we have a tremendous volume of goods to ship and there is a tremendous amount of money involved in freight charges. In that way we are indeed a captive market. That is so because the rates that the trucking and water transportation companies fix follow very closely, up or down, any revision in the railway rates. The minister is as well aware as I am that if there is a tremendous increase in railway rates there will be a corresponding increase in trucking and shipping rates in our area. Because of such actions on the part of the companies engaged in various methods of transportation I feel that special consideration should be given to our particular problems.
In regard to our particular area there is another factor which ought to be considered. I have spoken of the influx of industry which took place because the area was designated and thus enjoyed tax incentives. Though large corporations can obtain special rates, new industries in looking to this particular area as one in which to locate logically in order to take advantage of power and other facilities will be discouraged because they will

rates. As I say, there is the greatest fear in my area that since fabourable rates are to be retained in the west and in the mari-times-and I have no quarrel whatsoever with those special rates-the additional revenue will come mainly from the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, I offer no apology for intervening a second time in this debate on the clause by clause study. I consider that the debate which took place in the house before the Christmas recess was very useful and I commend the minister for his frank and honest answers. Similarly, I believe that hon. members on this side made useful and constructive suggestions. The interchange has made it easier for us to consider where we are and where we are going.
I may tell the minister at once that I propose to offer an amendment to clause 1, the clause now under study, in the firm belief that this legislation is somehow lacking. There is an element missing here, and it is one which is essential with respect to the legislation offered to this house and to the country as containing the elements of the national transportation policy needed to provide a better and fairer means of carrying goods and people between all parts of Canada.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
In offering this amendment to clause 1, which I understand is an indication to the commission to be established of the extent it should take into account a number of factors,

I do so because as I indicated earlier this commission will be venturing into uncharted courses like a spaceman reaching for one of the planets. It will come up against problems which it never has contemplated and which I am sure neither the minister nor those persons who drafted this bill have considered. All one needs to support this is to look at the report of proceedings and evidence of the committee. It is my belief that the element which is mentioned in this bill is one which has been the subject matter of a great number of directions. It has been the basis for inquiries made heretofore over a great number of years. I am speaking of the direction that the board have responsibilitiy for regulating and setting freight rates to provide for as great a measure of equalization as is possible within the very difficult circumstances which we have in this country because of the matters of geography and economies.
I do not care what is done; you cannot escape the fact that there is going to be some inequity and some discrimination. It will be impossible to reach that measure of equalization which we would like to see. Perfection in this aspect of our problems is not at all possible. I readily accede to that. However, under the existing law which we are to replace to some extent there were some attempts to eliminate this inequity and bring about equalization. I am referring to section 336 of the present Railway Act which, of course, will be eliminated by the provision we are now making.
A very brief historial record I think will help to place my views before the committee and indicate the reasons I am moving this amendment. In 1925 order in council P.C. 886 was passed by which the Board of Transport Commissioners was directed by the government to examine the freight rate structure and attempt to bring in harmony and provide for a measure of equity in all parts and regions of Canada. Later, in 1948, by order in council P.C. 1487, there was a further direction by the then government to the Board of Transport Commissioners.
The board of transport commissioners, in taking this responsibility, required a number of years to report. I do not think it was until some time in 1955 that they filed their report. At that time they made a statement which was quite correct. They said that equalization in Canada involved the establishment of a fundamental base and a statistical survey which would take many years of study to complete. The board of transport commissioners proceeded some distance along this
January 9, 1967

line and was successful in making certain suggestions. However, in the interval between the time the Board of Transport Commissioners was directed to do this and the time when they made their report, the same government established the royal commission which served under the late Mr. Justice Turgeon.

speechtext: He is still very much alive.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I am sorry. I should have said the former Mr. Justice Turgeon still very much alive as an individual. The recommendations in the report were brought in in 1950. They led to the amendment of the Railway Act in the second session of 1951. The minister may correct me if I am wrong, but I think it was in the second session of 1951 that section 336 of the present Railway Act was brought forth as being the answer in part to the suggestions and recommendations of Mr. Justice Turgeon and his commission.
Then we had the royal commission which was set up in 1959 by the Conservative government under the leadership of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. One of the terms of reference to the royal commission was that it report upon the inequities in the freight rate structure in Canada and so on. What I am pointing out is that if you examine one by one the various directions-these terms of reference-to the royal commissions and the directions to the Board of Transport Commissioners, you will see that there is a similar vein running through them in the form of a direction to them to examine the very serious problem regarding the inequities and the necessity of equalizing freight rates throughout Canada so far as possible in order to bring into closer alignment the disparities which have been created because of our geography.
Transportation policy, monetary policy and fiscal policy are the three weapons by which a government can partially bring together- lower the heights by raising the valleys- the different parts of the country. Certainly by no means the least of these is transportation policy. I should now like to repeat what I said when speaking on the resolution stage. I think it is necessary to do so because the commission which is to be established by Bill C-231 is directed in clause 1 in its activities and functions to carry out, under the same arrangements, the same directions, regulations and jurisdictions as the Board of Transport Commissioners now possesses. We are faced with the fact that, like the Board of Transport Commissioners, the commission
Transportation
which is now to be set up will establish its own jurisprudence and will be bound by these decisions.
As I pointed out once before, if you read the report of Mr. Justice Turgeon you will see quite readily that Mr. Justice Turgeon was very much of the opinion that the Board of Transport Commissioners, acting under the powers it then had, fell far short in its jurisdiction or power of trying to bring the equalization principle into effect. At page 23 of the royal commission report Mr. Justice Turgeon also said:
In the first decision of the hoard filed in the 30 per cent application on March 30, 1948, the position of the board with respect to its jurisdiction and powers to reduce rates to assist industry or to equalize, through the prescription of reduced rates, production costs, geographical location, or climatic conditions, was dealt with at considerable length.
The board said quite frankly that it did not think it had the power to do so. Again, at page 24-these are excerpts from the report of the royal commission-there is the following:
Railways are not required by law, and cannot in justice be required, to equalize natural disadvantages such as location, cost of production and the like.
Then, further on:
The board has many times said that it is not concerned with equalizing costs of production.
And again on this page:
It has been held time and again that rate-regulating commissions have no right whatever to attempt to equalize geographic, climatic, or economic conditions.
And so on. That is the situation. If this bill passes without any amendment, particularly to the declaration of policy enunciated in clause 1, we will be back in the same position because the present clause 68, which purports to deal with discrimination in rates, just and reasonable rates and so on, takes us right back to where we were prior to 1951 in that it says:
All tolls shall be just and reasonable and shall always, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions with respect to all traffic of the same description carried over the same route, be charged equally to all persons at the same rate.

I do not think it would be acceptable in the form in which it is now drafted. Perhaps I should deal first with my fears that if this amendment were incorporated in the bill it would certainly be a declaration that we should no
Transportation
longer have the Crowsnest pass rates, because if you equalize freight rates to the fullest extent possible the discrimination in rates in favour of wheat exports would have to go by the board. I think it would also create great fears in the Atlantic provinces that this was an attack upon the Maritime Freight Rates Act, even though it would not directly repeal that act. It would certainly indicate that parliament felt that this kind of discrimination -because that is precisely what the Maritime Freight Rates Act does; it discriminates in favour of that region to compensate for other disadvantages-should no longer take place.
Therefore, if one considers the phrase "to the fullest possible extent" I think there would be a feeling that a great many embedded discriminations, which I do not think anyone in the house is seriously arguing should be taken away-indeed the hon. member for Kent (Ont.), if I understood him correctly, seemed to suggest that there should be still another special consideration given to a region-would in fact be removed. I am not saying what the legal effect of the amendment would be; I would like to obtain legal advice before saying anything about that. But I think the effect it would tend to have would be that we would get rid of all these historic discriminations- and I use the word "discrimination" in its correct etymological sense-in favour of certain regions, and certain activities would no longer be within the spirit of the new transportation policy. That is something I could not consent to at all. I think it would be contrary to the whole spirit of the bill. I think, however, that objection could probably be overcome by a rewording of the amendment.
The other difficulty that I see at first glance-and I am putting these points forward so that members of the committee may consider them a little before we come to take a decision about the amendment which is now before us-is that it is going to be very difficult to apply such a provision. Most of us seem to accept this view in principle for every industry except the one we are interested in. I refer to the view that there should be the maximum amount of competition.
If anybody disliked the rates set as a result of competition, the presence of a phrase like

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words with regard to the transportation bill. First, since the minister has agreed with the amendment I suggested prior to the Christmas recess, perhaps it would be proper to allow him to word it so as to suit himself and the government, so I will leave that up to him.
There is another amendment which I should like to suggest to him but before doing so I would like to say a word or two about the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Peace River. Certainly I can speak wholeheartedly in favour of the suggestion made in this amendment because if it is followed through it will give more substance to clause 16. The general fault which I find with clause 16 is that it lacks certainty of protection against discrimination and also lacks a proper definition of the public interest. I am wholeheartedly in support of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Peace River.
However, my thoughts today lie more along the lines of competition. The minister has brought forward the bill in a rather hasty manner. I say this with due regard to Bill C-120 which was dropped two years ago and with due regard to the number of meetings
Transp ortation
held by the transport committee because it seems to me it is evident that this bill has been considerably amended. In fact some 65 to 70 amendments have been proposed and accepted by the minister which would point to the fact that insufficient consideration was given to the bill in the first place. Surely a bill which needs 70 amendments before being presented to the house is one to which insufficient prior thought was given in the initial stages of its drafting. While I do not lay the blame for this on the minister in particular I think that his staff should have drafted the bill more carefully so as to avoid the need for such a large number of amendments.
This bill brings together every mode of transportation in Canada, namely, railway, air, water, truck and even pipe lines. The theme of the bill is competition. If one really believes that competition will be the answer to our transportation problems in Canada then one must inject competition into every mode of transportation. But has this bill really achieved this? Clause 1(a) says that there shall be no regulations which will in any way restrict competition among the different modes of transport. Is this really enough? Does this clause really say that there shall be competition between the various carriers in any mode of transportation? It does not. This is why, after having given some thought to the matter during the Christmas recess, I once again put forward a suggestion which I made before the Christmas recess that perhaps we should implement an amendment suggested by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association as it appears in transport committee proceedings No. 27 on page 1926 and which provides that after the word "transport" in clause 1(a) the following words be added: "nor any carrier to compete freely with any other carrier".
If we really believe that competition is the answer I think we should state that there shall not be any regulations restricting competition between one carrier and another. Surely this follows particularly with regard to the railroad and trucking industries, if trucks are to fall under this legislation and if clause 1 of the bill is really intended to deal with every mode of transportation. As I read this particular part of clause 1 it refers to any mode of transportation. We must therefore state that we will not allow regulations which will restrict competition among the carriers in any mode of transportation. I should like the minister to consider this suggestion because I think I will move it as an amendment before clause 1 is agreed to.

January 9, 1967
Transportation
I should also like the minister to give some thought to competition in every mode of transportation in Canada. What does this bill do with regard to railroads? If railroads are not included they will continue to set rates which are not necessarily competitive. What does the bill do with regard to air transportation? It does nothing. The Air Transport Board and the Aeronautics Act are included under the bill which, however, does not incorporate competition in this field in any real sense.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
This bill does not touch Air Canada and leaves that company in a monopoly position all across Canada. It does not say that in the future steps will be taken to bring about a greater degree of competition.
It is interesting to note that during the committee proceedings Mr. Crump of the C.P.R. made a statement which appears in report of committee proceedings No. 28 at page 2009. I am not going to read it, but he stated that air cargo is developing into a very significant factor in intercity ton miles. I am paraphrasing what he said. There is no denying the fact that passenger traffic on air lines has increased tremendously during the last ten years. It is my belief, as it is Mr. Crump's, that in the next ten years air freight is going to increase to the same degree.
What does this bill do with regard to air freight? It does very little, if anything. Surely we cannot continue to say that this commission is going to regulate all modes of transportation when the bill does nothing with regard to air freight except transplant the machinery of the Aeronautics Act to this commission. The bill does not touch Air Canada at all. Certainly one of the significant factors in this regard is that Air Canada does not have any competition. If competition is the real theme of this bill, then we should seek some avenue in the bill which in the years ahead would provide a road for greater competition in air freight and air passenger travel as well as air transportation generally.
Every other air line, whether it be a little one operating between Regina and Calgary or Trans-Air in eastern Canada, has to apply for a licence under the Aeronautics Act or I suppose to the new commission that this bill will set up. However, Air Canada can operate all across Canada without applying for a licence and can discontinue a service without anything more than a public hearing. We saw that very thing take place on the prairies a few years ago.

This bill does very little, if anything, to bring about any degree of competition in air traffic, whether it be air freight or passenger travel. Let us not fool ourselves by saying that this bill brings all modes of transportation under one commission. The verbiage in the bill may well be to that effect, but it does nothing to bring about any adjustment of the conditions in which we now find ourselves with regard to air traffic. One only has to think back to the recent strike of Air Canada personnel to realize that transportation was severely tied up in Canada. More costly ways had to be found to move many of the perishable commodities which have normally moved by Air Canada. I should like to see some avenue created in this bill by which in the years ahead steps could be taken to create a greater degree of competition in air passenger travel and air freight. We should recognize the fact that there is room for such competition in Canada.
What does this bill do with regard to water transportation? There is a provision to the effect that transport by water, which falls under the Transport Act and is generally under the jurisdiction of the federal government, will fall under this new commission. What was the government's attitude just a year ago with regard to the competitive factor in northern Alberta? The government bought out its only competition on the McMurray waterways. At that time Northern Transportation, a government company, bought out Yellowknife Transportation for some $2.5 million. It was the only competition the government company had. Was that any way for a government to act which now comes to us and purports to believe that competition is the answer to our transportation problems in this country? They are not holding true to their belief of a year ago when they felt they had to buy out competition in order to survive. Today the government purports to believe that we must return to competition.
Let us look at truck competition. The minister says we are going to include a clause, I think in part III or perhaps part II of this bill, which will deal solely with truck competition. Without the amendment suggested by the Canadian Manufacturers Association, how does clause 1 apply to truck transport? We should state quite clearly that we will not allow any regulations which will restrict competition among carriers. This is a very strong point with regard to truck traffic because if you look at the major trucking concerns in Canada which operate from the maritimes through to western Canada you find you can
January 9, 1967

name them on the fingers of both hands. Most of them are owned by the two railroads. Therefore we should not allow any regulations that would prohibit free competition among carriers in the trucking industry. I firmly believe that the amendment suggested by the Canadian Manufacturers Association is necessary in order to safeguard competition within the trucking industry.
During the proceedings of the transport committee we tried to find out the percentage of long-haul trucking services which the railroads really owned. We were not forceful enough in the committee to ascertain just what that percentage really was. There was some indication that this information could not be given out. The trucking association presented a brief to the committee and stated they would like to have that information but they could not really ascertain it. One of the great handicaps under which the transport committee worked was that the committee was not given enough facts to ascertain the value of this bill when one considers the fact that according to the bill competition is the answer to all our transportation problems.
Many people in Canada believe that there is not enough competition between the large trucking concerns because the Canadian National alone, I believe, owns practically outright over half a dozen trucking firms and Canadian Pacific must own a similar number. When you ascertain how many trucking firms there are, for instance, operating in the mari-times you realize that there is little real competition. If one were to project that thinking into other areas of Canada, I am sure one would come to the same conclusion.
With regard to the commodity pipe line aspect of this bill I believe this amendment should be included. The Shell Oil Company presented a brief with regard to commodity pipe lines. This company believes that commodity pipe lines really need not come under this bill because there is no such thing in Canada yet and pipe lines will come under two federal boards, the National Energy Board, which in most cases will regulate the commodity in the pipe line, and this new commission which will regulate the transportation aspect of that commodity. Pipe lines are a means of transportation whether they carry oil or whether they carry sulphur. If jurisdiction over a pipe line carrying oil is with the National Energy Board, I see no reason why that same board could not regulate the
Transportation
charges made for the transportation of sulphur as well as the charges made for the transportation of oil.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
After all, Mr. Chairman, the least government is the best government. That is a principle which is generally accepted in a free society. But what is taking place in this bill? We are including in the bill a clause dealing with commodity pipe lines when we do not have any commodity pipe lines in Canada and when we do not know what commodity pipe lines system will be used in Canada. We are projecting our thinking into the future and are saying that we should have another regulatory body to govern such pipe lines when we already have the necessary machinery to handle them at the initial stage. I see the minister shakes his head but let him hear me out first.
It may well be, Mr. Chairman, that if these pipe lines should develop into a well-accepted means of transportation there would then be ample time to bring in any required legislation. I did ask the minister whether there had been any prior consultation with the provinces about trucks and commodity pipe lines and the minister replied that he would have meetings with the provinces in this regard.
Why do we include a clause in a federal bill dealing with the trucking industry, which is mainly a provincial matter though not entirely, without prior consultation with the provinces? Where is the co-operative federalism we heard so much about two years ago which was going to solve all our problems? The government was going to have ample prior consultation with the provinces on every matter of concern to them.
What have we seen in this house since that time, Mr. Chairman? We have been asked to pass one piece of legislation after another on the pretence that after this house had passed it the government would consult the provinces as to their views. Where, oh where has that co-operative federalism gone? It is certainly not evident in this bill.
As I said in my initial remarks on this bill, I believe that both the government and the minister have proceeded too hastily with the bill and have not consulted the provinces to any extent. They drafted a bill which required some 70 odd amendments and there may yet be further amendments. Surely if some thought had been given to the drafting of the bill and prior consultation had been had with the provinces about the trucking

January 9, 1967
Transportation
industry and commodity pipe lines, the government would have presented a bill which would have been readily acceptable to the house, the provinces and the people of Canada in general. I can only hope that in the coming week or weeks we will be able to iron out the problems in this bill so that some good will come out of it. Either that or the minister should withdraw it altogether and redraft the bill in light of the amendments proposed and the amendments which have been already accepted.

The hon. member for Qu'Appelle made a very powerful argument for rationalization of the railways, with a large part of which I completely agree, with a view to reducing, in the interests of the economy and the efficient transportation of grain competition, which is of the wasteful sort.

The hon. gentleman knows that the whole intention of the Aeronautics Act has been to provide competition where there is enough traffic to warrant it, to make sure that in the case of regional carriers and others there should be adequate scope to operate effectively and to enable them to make a financial success of their operations, and to avoid the kind of cut-throat competition which would make it impossible for any of them to operate effectively.
The hon. gentleman said that we were not amending the Air Canada Act in this bill. We are not amending the Canadian National Railways Act or a great many other statutes either. We are laying down certain general principles.
When the hon. gentleman's friends were in office they did permit a limited amount of competition on main air lines, and I have indicated that this government has no intention of changing that policy. Indeed, I am hopeful that in the very near future I will be able to make a statement with respect to that matter.

The hon. gentleman made three points, two of which I have dealt with and the third I have not. I think what we are seeking to do in this general statement in clause 1 is not to lay down particular rules for the railways, for the air lines or for any other particular mode of transport. What we are trying to do is to lay down guide lines for competition between those modes of transport and for the relationships between them.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in these circumstances we would be making more difficulties for ourselves than we would solve by attempting to change this particular subclause in the manner suggested by the hon. member. We do have very keen competition now between the railways and there is certainly very keen competition between the two air lines wherever they are allowed to compete. I do not think we need insist on this kind of competition in this legislation. What we are seeking to do is to make it possible for the various modes of transport to compete.
While I am on my feet, though this does not relate to clause 1 at all perhaps I could say a few words about each of the other two points raised by the hon. gentleman. First with regard to commodity pipe lines there is no provision in the law of Canada at the present time for commodity pipe lines, apart from pipe lines to carry oil and gas. It was the view of the government that some provision should be made the first time appropriate legislation was brought before parliament to meet that gap, and it is a gap in legislation. I think it is appropriate to meet this gap in the way it is being met in this bill, which will not involve any double jurisdiction at all. A commodity pipe line that does not carry gas or oil will be exclusively under the jurisdiction of the new commission.

draftsman and did not know its own business, but if it does not accept amendments it is stubborn, obstinate and arrogant. You have to pay your money and take your choice. No matter what course you take the opposition will do nothing but condemn you.
We are, I hope, nearly through the rhetorical aspects of clause 1. Perhaps we can get down to the bill and forget how many amendments there are. The highway situation is somewhat different. Parliament 10 or 12 years ago passed legislation when the Privy Council decided that this parliament, and not the provincial legislatures, had jurisdiction over interprovincial and international trucking. This parliament has legislation empowering the provincial boards to act as federal agents. Many people do not understand that they act as federal agents. They have no power conferred on them by the legislatures. That could not be done. Such power can only be conferred by this parliament. To the extent that this delegation will continue to work there is no disposition to change it. But we have some reason to believe, because of certain decisions the courts have made, that some of these provincial agencies will not be able effectively to carry on their task. This is a matter about which the provincial governments, of course, should be consulted because they have allowed their agencies to act for us until now. The provincial governments should be consulted in due course about whether a change should be made. I do not think that provincial governments should be asked their views about the legislation-the legislative act is exclusively within the jurisdiction of this parliament-any more than we should expect the government of Alberta or any other province to consult us before introducing legislation exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature.
Where the division of authority is completely clear it seems to me that on the whole we get along better if we mind our own business. Whether it is advisable to give this reserve power to this new commission is something we can discuss when we come to the clause dealing with it. The same holds true with respect to pipe lines. Both these matters in my view show deficiencies in the general law at the present time that it is desirable to correct.

Mr. Chairman, if it will not come as too great a shock to the minister I wish to commend him on his flexibility in agreeing to accept some of the amendments proposed in the committee. No one can accuse the minister of having gone hastily into the preparation of this bill when one looks at its genesis in the days of the MacPherson Royal Commission appointed by the previous administration.
Having said that, I wish to comment about the extraordinary piece of verbiage the minister has included in clause 1 of the bill. This is a most amazing piece of drafting. One might consider the language as the preamble to the bill. If one turns the page and sees the short title referred to in clause 2, one might be pardoned for thinking that the language in clause 1 is the preamble to the bill. The more I have looked at clause 1 the more I have become convinced that the minister's thought about a new transportation policy has gone down the drain.
As I read clause 1 it virtually assures that the new transportation commission the bill seeks to establish will continue to flounder in the sea of misunderstanding and illogicality that has prevailed in the Canadian transportation system over a great many years. In clause 1 the minister, it seems to me, has most effectively sought to perpetuate the confusion in which our transportation system has found itself for a long time.
The bill starts with these words:
An Act to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada-

January 9, 1967
Transportation
That is high-sounding. I have no objection to ministers introducing bills with high-sounding titles. It is within the bounds of reasonable ambition on their parts to have bills with high-sounding titles on the statute books to perpetuate their memories.
When one reads the first sentence of what I call the preamble, because it is not properly clause 1 as I define it, one sees this statement:
It is hereby declared that an economic and efficient transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest total cost is essential to the economic well-being and growth of Canada-
Few Canadians will find much to disagree with in that statement. But when one goes beyond that one immediately enters into the strange realm of thought that has prevailed for all too long, that some mystic benefit is to be derived from competition in transportation. I listened to the hon. member for Acadia, who obviously wallows in the quagmire in which the minister wallows. Some people think that if we could have competition, if we could get 25 railway companies to build lines across Canada to transport goods cheaply, somehow or other we should have an efficient transportation system working in the interests of all transportation users in Canada. That is the attitude that has prevailed. I am no authority on railway history, but if we look back in history I am sure we will find that it was the kind of philosophy I have just alluded to that forced the government of Canada in other days to set up the Canadian National Railways.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
In spite of all this experience, this myth about the value of competition as being basic to the efficient functioning of transportation in Canada is being perpetuated, indeed, enforced in an act of parliament by virtue of clause 1 of this bill. This is the situation which has produced the conflicts to which I have been listening between supporters of the government and members of the official opposition. The minister has pointed out that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle contends there should be a greater degree of control over the railways to ensure that grain rates remain low. I hear voices from the maritimes in favour of moves to ensure that the maritime freight rates subsidy should continue. Now the hon. member for Peace River has introduced an amendment which in some ways I find to be laudable. But I would suggest to the hon. member for Peace River that his attempt to bring reason and order into what is contained in clause 1 is a hopeless effort. All it is likely

to do is to add to the confusion which already exists.
To my mind the basic situation is clear. The best way of ensuring an efficient transportation system in Canada is to bring about a system whereby all modes of transportation and all the vehicles used complement one another instead of indulging in unnecessary and fruitless competition. It is through this approach that we are likely to get the most effective and economic system of transportation best suited to the needs of the people of this country. I suggest to the minister that the best thing he could do would be to remove clause 1 entirely and renumber clause 2 as clause 1. We could then consider the bill from that point. As things stand, all we are doing in effect is to ensure from the very start that the transportation commission will be unable to function in the manner proposed in clause 14.
I put it to the minister that there is an inherent contradiction between what is set out in clause 1 and what is contained in clause 14 as to the powers and duties of the proposed commission. In order to illustrate my point I will quote the relevant part of clause 14.
It is the duty of the Commission to perform the functions vested in the Commission by this Act, the Railway Act, the Aeronautics Act and the Transport Act with the object of co-ordinating and harmonizing the operations of all carriers engaged in transport by railways, water, aireraft, extraprovincial motor vehicle transport and commodity pipelines;
Here we find set out what I consider to be a realistic transportation idea. Unfortunately the idea that the duty of the commission is to co-ordinate and harmonize the operations of all carriers is completely nullified by the terms of clause 1 where we find it stated that these objectives are most likely to be achieved when all modes of transport are able to compete-a contention which maintains and perpetuates the paradoxical transportation policy which has prevailed for far too long in this country.
I know that when he introduced the bill the minister urged strongly that it be allowed to go to the committee where its details could be studied. Many of us were prepared for that to happen. In fact we expedited the passage of the bill to the point at which it could be sent to committee for that purpose, recognizing that certain changes were long overdue particularly with respect to the operations of the national railways.
I do not profess to be in a position to discuss in detail the proposals contained in this bill with respect to railways operations. Some of my hon. friends who are more directly
