Mr. Chairman, this evening I am going to address my remarks to the

January 9, 1967
Transportation
amendment put forward by the hon. member for Peace River. Once again I am very pleased that the Minister of Transport is here because these remarks will be basic to the decision he will be attempting to arrive at between seven and eight o'clock vis-a-vis the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River. The amendment of the hon. member for Peace River is an effort on the part of the Conservative opposition to try to give guide lines to the new transportation commission which will help them make their judicial decisions. It is similar to subclauses (a), (b) and (c) of clause 1.
I should like to read part of the amendment again:
-it is essential to recognize the policy of equalization of freight rates to the fullest possible extent as a means of dealing equitably with all parts of Canada-
In respect of the first part of the amendment concerning the question of equalization,
I have pointed out before and I should like to repeat that there is nothing which has bothered the people of Canada more than the question of equalization. Throughout the years, particularly in the maritimes and in the prairies, the unfairness inherent in the fact that it costs so much more to ship goods on the railways for a certain distance in the prairies and the maritimes than it does to ship them the same distance in the central provinces has been one of the great economic injustices which have divided this country.
This bill is an attempt to bring the railways up to full efficiency by permitting competition in the field of transportation between the railways on the one hand and other modes of transportation on the other. I believe the great majority of the people of Canada are willing to give a try to this policy of competition. On the other hand, since we are realistic we know that railways, truckers, air lines and others forms of transportation have not endeared themselves to the people of Canada in the past by evidence that they were honestly competing. There is too much evidence to the contrary. There is a good reason for this being so. The railways in effect are a type of semimonopoly. When a railway goes through a certain area, in effect it provides the only service in that area. When you have a location in Canada where the competition is very keen, where railways run reasonably close together and where you also have water, air and truck transportation, you can visualize a situation where there is honest and genuine competition. There still are many areas in Canada,
[Mr. Hamilton.!
however, where in reality that guarantee cannot be given.
The phrase, "equalization of freight rates" is a clear direction from parliament and I think gives an axe to the minister and the new transportation commission. In recognition of the way competition works we have included the phrase, "to the fullest possible extent".
I think that phrase gives sufficient leeway that the transportation commission can recognize in some areas that the equalization principle will have to be departed from.
One of the situations of which we all have knowledge is that in respect of the Panama Canal. It is a matter of common knowledge that you can ship goods from Montreal to Vancouver by water in competition with the movement of freight by rail from Montreal to Vancouver. Therefore, in order to give competition in that type of situation between modes of transportation the transportation commission would have to permit a type of freight rate which would allow the railways, one mode of transportation, to compete effectively with another mode, that of water. This, however, does not ease the pain for the people of Regina or Calgary who know that the freight rates they pay for rail transportation are so much higher than they are when the same goods are moved from Montreal to Vancouver. When it is cheaper to ship a particular article from Montreal to Vancouver than from Montreal to Calgary it is natural that the people will raise the cry of discrimination and nonequalization. As the hon. member for Peace River pointed out, royal commissions have tried to tackle this problem but have failed to come up with a precise answer. All we in parliament can do is suggest, as this amendment attempts to do, that the commission wherever possible provide an equalization of freight rates.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
Obviously if there is to be competition between the three, four or five railway companies in Canada the rates cannot be precisely the same. Let me give some examples of what I mean in an attempt to explain possible situations which may still exist following the adoption of the this bill. I have given these examples in general principle on previous occasions.
Clause 68 is very carefully worded so as not to force the railway companies or the transportation commission to provide equalization of freight rates. In clause 68 under the heading "Traffic, Tolls and Tariffs" we find that subsection (1) of new section 381 states:
January 9, 1967

All tolls shall be just and reasonable and shall always, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions with respect to all traffic of the same description carried over the same route, be charged equally to all persons at the same rate.
On first reading that it looks like it provides for equalization of rates, but when you reread it in light of our experience over the last 40 years there is a loophole for discrimination provided by the phrase "carried over the same route". The words that are missing, of course, are "the same distance". We have tried by our amendment to include words which will indicate to the transportation commission that we want to achieve the major objective of this bill, namely, competition, while at the same time eliminate any possibility of discrimination.
Let me provide a hypothetical example. Suppose a particular item is being transported from Winnipeg a distance of 130 miles west to the city of Brandon at a rate which is lower than that applying to the transportation of the same item 130 miles from Winnipeg east to the city of Kenora. That situation could well exist within the terms of this bill but it would be discriminatory against the people of Kenora. Conversely, if the rate were higher to Brandon than to Kenora, it would be discriminatory against the people of Brandon. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Peace River, which is being held in abeyance, was designed to prevent this type of discrimination from occurring by the inclusion of the words "to the fullest possible extent".
Let me propose another example. The majority of development in Canada in the future will take place in the paper and mining industries in our northern areas. At this time 90 per cent of our population live in a narrow strip in the southern part of the country within 10 per cent of our total area. A great majority of our transportation problems in future will relate to various methods of transportation from our newly developed areas. Under clause 68 of this bill it would be possible for railway companies, without in any way infringing upon the principles, to establish different rates for hauling similar ore from different locations over an equal distance.
Let me use Winnipeg again for the purposes of my example. If a mine were developed a specific distance to the northeast of Winnipeg and a similar mine were developed to the north of Winnipeg, provided the product was the same and the distance to the concentrator was the same the same rate should apply.
T ransportation
Similar ore collected at the one mine and carried over the same distance as ore collected from the other mine should be moved for exactly the same rate. Under the provisions of this bill a different rate could be charged. Let me enlarge somewhat on this example. If ore were being transported from a mine in northern Quebec to a concentrator at a higher rate than ore transported from a mine to Winnipeg, to Sault Ste. Marie, Port Arthur or Fort William, provided the distances were the same the people in Quebec would feel they were being discriminated against. On the other hand, if the rate in Quebec was lower the people in Manitoba or Ontario would feel discriminated against.
In view of the realities it is not possible to obtain complete equalization of rates. There may well be competitive factors involved. We have taken this into consideration in drafting our amendment. That is why we suggest there should be equalization of freight rates "to the fullest possible extent".
It is my hope that the minister and his officials will realize that we are not attempting to be obstructive in moving this amendment. What we are attempting to do is to make it clear to the commission that parliament desires equalization of freight rates to the fullest extent possible. We must take into consideration competitive factors, but if those factors are relatively equal there is little reason why the rates cannot be equal.
We have attempted to protect the various modes of transportation in this country. We have done so effectively by stating that no mode of transportation can charge a rate below cost. That provides a basic protection to every mode of transportation. But what have we done to protect the user? Users must realize that there is some body, in this case the national transportation commission, which has been directed by parliament to make sure as fai as possible that similar goods carried a similar distance by a similar transportation system are carried at the same rate.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I think I have made my point sufficiently, and I hope fairly enough, to indicate that we are not trying to cause trouble for the minister or the people who will have to redraft this amendment. We are trying to arrive at something that will indicate to the national transportation commission that we are attempting to get over the old bugaboo of d scrimination which has plagued and divided this country for so long. We are doing this to show the committee something they should

January 9, 1967
Transportation
already know, namely, how serious this discrimination has been. Up to the year 1957, I believe, since the war increases in freight rates have been granted by the Governor General in Council amounting to 150 per cent. The whole burden of th:s tremendous increase in freight rates fell on the prairies and the maritimes and those areas apart from the competitive area between Montreal and Toronto. It did not bear on the people in the competitive areas.
I have already said that we cannot get rid of discrimination entirely, but as our country develops more and more in the northern areas this tremendous dissatisfaction will continue unless there is some assurance that the board to which we are giving these tremendous powers is working in the interests of the user. This is why there will be a great deal of trouble in regard to the definition of "public interest". Does "public interest" simply imply that you have competition between the railways regardless of the fairness to the user? If that is the motivation or theory behind this bill, it will cause just as much trouble as previous efforts by parliament to try and get out of this rut. We are trying to be helpful by suggesting what I think is a fairly constructive amendment which does not limit to the fullest extent the power of the new commission to do the right thing. But they should know that parliament is holding them responsible to try to arrive at the maximum amount of equalization possible.
In this bill we are telling the people of Canada that parliament will look after their interests properly and that the national transportation commission will defend those interests. But the public interest must, by the very nature of things, not only be loyal to the principle of competition but loyal to the reality of competition and the fact that in the end result we are trying to serve the user as fairly as possible.
I have one more point to make which is in harmony with what I have said in the house on previous occasions with regard to rationalization. I suggested to the house on second reading that one of our purposes in this b'U should be to give the commission more power, the power to direct, the power to achieve positive purposes. Then at the committee stage I supported another amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River suggesting that this board, with all its powers, should have some controls placed on it. Those two viewpoints are not contradictory. They are, I think, realist'c and practicable.

If we want to run our transportation system efficiently, it seems that we have to turn it over to a highly skilled board that can deal with it. This is the essence of the bill. But if we turn all these powers over to the board, not only should we in the drafting of the bill try to state our aims and objectives in the form of guide lines to the board but we should have some way of touching base with them occasionally. That is why we in the official opposition have suggested that there should be set up by statute some form of institutional framework which would guarantee to the people whose interests we are placing in the hands of this commission that their representatives in parliament will every year have to examine carefully what the board is doing.
In summary, Mr. Chairman, we are turning over more power to the board. I would even give it more power than this bill gives, namely, the power to direct as well as to recommend. At the same time I want to strengthen control over the board in a way which will not interfere with its efficiency in handling our transportation system. This amendment is not as fundamental as the earlier one, but I think it meets the long-standing grievance of the people in those areas which have been most discriminated against, northern Ontario, northern Quebec, the prairies and the maritimes. They will at least feel that we in parliament are giving the board, proper guide lines in this field.
If we try to tie the direction down to dollars and cents and precise details, it will destroy the purpose of the bill. We should set out our aims and objectives in such a way that will direct the board but leave some loophole whereby the railways can adapt themselves to the competitive position of different areas and within reason make the adjustments that are necessary.
We cannot reach the most perfect situation in the world but at least we want the people whom we represent and who have been discriminated against over the years to feel that a case is being made on their behalf. I believe that in this opening clause it would help a little if we included some phraseology that would give the assurance that the board was directed by parliament in an attempt to arrive at our objectives, rather than including such a provision in the section of the bill covering the powers of the board. If we included this amendment at least the people would know that periodically we will see that these things are carried out to the fullest extent possible as far as members of parliament are concerned
January 9, 1967

in trying to set up legislation and maintain the right of the people to have some control over their masters.
The final point I wish to make deals with positive thinking and positive approaches. I believe in what I call dynamic, positive government. I believe we have an opportunity in this bill, in which we are delegating powers in respect of transportation to a national commission, to try to use this Canadian Transport Commission as part of national policy. I know that for many decades to come things will have to be done in the field of transportation that do not come under the ordinary* rules of competitive private enterprise. I know that by roads, highways, air routes and possibly pipe lines we will have to open up our country by moving transportation into areas where there is no immediate monetary return to the carriers. I know that for periods of years, and perhaps decades, some of these operations will have to run at a loss.
We have agreed with the principle enunciated by the MacPherson Royal Commission that, if we ask any mode of transportation to take on these national functions, any losses wifi be recompensed from the national treasury. What I am trying to say is included in this amendment. I refer to the phrase "equalization of freight rates to the fullest possible extent as a means of dealing equitably with all parts of Canada and as being the method best calculated to facilitate the interchange of commodities between the various parts of the country"-and this is the part I want to emphasize-"as well as the encouragement of industry and agriculture in all regions and the development of export trade."
That last phrase is the positive one. We are there saying that the national transportation commission must have as its guide line in the national interest the developing of exports, our mining industry, our paper industry and even the agricultural industry. Many Canadians have not yet recognized that the last great backstop of all the hungry people of the world will be in northern Canada and northern Russia.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
The great muskegs, with the greatest soil productivity in the world, will be the base from which we will feed the hungry millions. Even if one is accused of looking too far into the future, the Canadian Transport Commission, under this amendment as a guide line, will know that they have the responsibility of looking into the future and of proposing to air lines, pipe line companies, railroads and
Transportation
even water transportation around our coasts, that in the interests of developing our country they can make proposals to the agencies they govern.
I think all this is made possible in the amendment, and I hope that when the minister meets his officials between 7 and 8 p.m. today he and they will recognize that the additional paragraph we have proposed is put forward without any intention to interfere with the principle of competition. It also has the purpose of trying to carry out what I think every Canadian would like to see, namely a maximum equalization of freight rates. I have been very candid in saying that under certain circumstances one cannot provide perfect equalization, but there are so many cases of discrimination that it would be good to know that this transportation commission is actively watching and seeking at all times to end or reduce that discrimination.
Finally I shall repeat a point I have made already, that I would like to see an active, dynamic government which would not interfere with private enterprise. If this transport commission could do a certain amount of projection of the national policy, then the government would have through this commission a way of getting things done-something we have found very difficult in the past.
I know the minister does not wish to re-live that awful debate on the Pine Point railway. That was a classic example where private enterprise, in this case in the form of the Canadian Pacific Railway, did not see the obvious truth that there would be a need for certain mineral products in a short space of time, and refused to build a railway line to its own mining properties. The government of Canada of the day had to put money behind the Canadian National Railways to get this line built. Is it not a wonderful thing that we did it? Certainly we made money for the C P-R., and all those who had invested in the Pine Point mines reaped large benefits. But the main thing was that we saved this country hundreds of thousands of dollars of foreign exchange and we saved it from having to import these minerals at much higher prices.
This was a good policy at that time. The private enterprise did not see the necessity for it, but thank heavens we had a government which believed in this country and believed in taking dynamic action. I hope that the Canadian Transport Commission will be composed of people who will read into the amendment and into the remarks made in the house the meaning which we intend, namely that we hope they have some red corpuscles in their

January 9, 1967
Transportation
blood stream, and some adrenalin to enable them to take the dynamic action we hope such a board will take when national interests are at stake.

speechtext: I would like to put one question to the hon. gentleman for clarification, if he would permit me to do it. As I understand his interpretation of the purpose of the amendment, in so far as equalization is concerned-I am not talking about the other more visionary aspects which he mentioned in the latter part of his speech-it is not intended in any way to inhibit the railways or any other mode of transport from meeting competition, but is merely intended to say that in areas where there is no competition there should not be discrimination as between one part of the country and another. I do not know whether I made myself clear.

I think we are in agreement. As you know, rates are set for a certain product in a certain area, and no one ever examines them from year to year. These discriminatory rate structures remain for ever and ever. I was hoping this amendment would make it clear to the Canadian Transport Commission that their job is to try to set rates wherever possible on the basis of equalization, rather than on the basis of phraseology contained in clause 68, which deals with section 381 (1).
The other point I wish to make is that I think it is wrong in principle to worship the theory of competition to such a degree that you give to a private company, whether it is the C.P.R., the C.N.R. or the P.G.E., the right to decide what the freight rate will be for a certain new development as opposed to another new development. This, in the name of competition, gives too much power to the private company. If the Canadian Transport Commission were on the alert for this type of thing, it could be prevented. One can imagine that, with the interlocking directorates, and with the C.P.R. which is engaged in many forms of enterprise, if one of these enterprises belonged to the circle of their companies and another set of enterprises belonged to the competitive company, discrimination could occur.
I do not want to impute bad motives or to suggest that the railway would deliberately set a special rate to help their boys a little bit more than the others, but I would like to believe there was a referee or a judicial court set up to stop this sort of thing, unless there were good reasons for establishing lower rates at one point than at another. The principle

should remain, that similar goods travelling the same distances should be treated in the same way.
In the case of the oil and gas industry, we do not bother with these details in legislation. We simply say to the pipe lines and to the gas distribution companies in the provinces: You are a semi-monopoly, but we watch you by setting the maximum rate of return on the capital which is usually set on the basis of the rate base. We allow these companies to compete and to do what they like pricewise because their competition has to be met in various areas. For example in Ontario there is discrimination in the gas rates, but the government controls them simply by making it very clear in the regulations what their maximum rate of return can be.
We have not set up this system in this bill. If we do not set up a system of maximum returns-which would be too difficult to attempt in the case of the railways-we have to put a finger of control down here and there, and that is what I think this amendment will do. If the transportation commission is aware that as far as possible parliament wishes to get rid of discrimination, then a great cause of disunity and unfairness will be removed.

I can assure the hon. gentleman that if my enunciation of the proposition was the one he had in mind, that is precisely the objective of the government. I wonder if I could repeat my objection for the minister so that it might be considered during the supper recess? The hon. member for Peace River has put forward this amendment which recommends a recognition of the policy of equalization of freight rates to the fullest extent as a means of developing all parts of Canada. The amendment is akin to the complaint of some of us from the maritimes, that in embarking on this national transportation policy we somehow are putting aside the national policy of using transportation to develop the regions of Canada that have not been as fortunate as others, in so far as competition in transportation is concerned.
One of the objections the minister made to this amendment was that it might not consider the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the statutory protection that the maritimes have. Whether that is true, I do not know. However, perhaps we should place in the legislation, either in this or some other clause, the amendment which I suggested should be seriously considered. On an earlier occasion I felt it was important, but it is taking on a greater significance in my mind now, and I will tell the minister in a minute why that is so.
Transportation
The amendment to which I refer is the one put forward by the Maritime Transportation Commission, when they made their presentation to the committee which considered this bill. That commission suggested that after section 1(b), the following words should be added, "except as may otherwise be necessary for constitutional, statutory or national policy purposes." If those words were in the bill, the objection the minister has to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River might be covered. This amendment also appeals to me because it ties in with the study that has taken place on maritime transportation problems. We have to buy a pig in a poke or pray that something is going to come up in the future.
I suggest that if these words are in the bill, then a future government will have to recognize this protection, whereas if these words are not there an entirely different method could be adopted for dealing with the transportation problems of the maritimes. I am not suggesting future governments would not be aware of this, and I frankly told the minister that I wondered whether we should put a full time order on this freeze. Although I cannot speak for my colleagues, I am quite willing to take a chance that there would be enough pressure from the maritimes to cause the government to act.
If there is not some statement in this bill to the effect that we recognize in this parliament that national policy as a means of providing transportation facilities en an equitable basis for every region is protected, then I am afraid a new government might not consider that aspect and might use something different on an experimental basis. I think the minister has my thought. Perhaps he will be able to work in something that will satisfy himself in connection with the weakness of this amendment and also make many maritimers happy in the knowledge that it has been stated that all will agree with a national policy on transportation as separate from a new national transportation policy.
There are one or two other points which perhaps I could develop at this time. They arise from some of the problems we discussed before the Christmas recess and about which we have had a chance to think further. Some hon. members have paid tribute to the minister's flexibility and good intentions. I did that in the committee. I think we will have to test these statements against the proceedings in the house on the bill. It has been said that we need definite direction, and that words are

Transportation
important in a section such as we are considering because the new transport board will be reading these words rather carefully and trying to ascertain exactly what we intended.
We all know that the minister is flexible, is good natured and that certain things are intended. Flour offers a good example of the difficulty of putting these intentions into legislative form. Everybody in the committee agreed that we wanted to provide the same protection for flour as there had been. I am not an expert in the matter, but I understand when the new legislation was brought forward flour was excluded from many of the provisions that affected grain. We were all desirous of at least putting flour in the position it was before. It would seem to me, as a layman, that since the west grows the grain and mills some of the flour and the east benefits from these lucrative flour shipments through eastern ports, everybody should be interested in Canada as a nation milling and shipping as much flour as possible. Two amendments have come forward, and they were put forward fairly. Everybody considered them. I understand now there is some difficulty in connection with the second amendment, in that some flour mills were not included. Unless changes are made, this might drastically affect about 50 per cent of the business that has been going through most of the eastern ports.
I know the minister and his officials are considering the matter, so I do not want my words to be taken as criticism of any departmental or railway officials who may be considering this matter. I just want to use it as an example of the fact that it is not easy to put into legislative form for all time the exact intent in providing a cure for these problems.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
Another matter that came to my mind was this question of port parity. I understand we are still going to hear from the minister on this subject. Perhaps on that occasion he will give us a better indication of how that affects Saint John and whether the rates vis-a-vis the United States ports are going to be protected. I read in the paper the other day the industrial port commissioner in Quebec city, who of course is trying to promote business, made the flat statement that it is $14 per ton cheaper to ship newsprint through Quebec than through Saint John. He went on to say that this is an argument each shipper in Quebec should be able to count on, and that therefore winter navigation should be kept open. I see the minister is smiling but he has no need to

worry; I am not going to get into the subject of winter navigation at the moment. I have already put substantial argument on the record over the years in this regard.
If this is true, I do not know whether any agreed charges are involved. I would assume the longshoremen would form a comparable category because they are now on identical rates. If it is true that it is $14 per ton cheaper to ship newsprint through Quebec than through Saint John, then there is something wrong with our freight rate structure. The very reason out province went into confederation, Mr. Chairman, was to get equalized rates so that we could be competitive. If these are taken away from us, then even without winter navigation I do not know what hope there is for us in the future. This thought occurred to me during the holidays when I was trying to be fair minded and was viewing the matter on a broad, national basis.
One other subject on which I think the minister should try to obtain more information concerns the freeze on the maritime freight rates. I am confused about this question, which is looming fairly large. As I stated in my earlier remarks, I think we would do better to put a time limit on this freeze. I have perused some of the records in this connection, and when we come to the particular clause I should like to have an indication of how much of our traffic is affected by this freeze. The departmental officials seemed to minimize it, and I am sorry I do not have before me their exact words. At the same time, in reply to me the other day the minister said that quite a substantial part of our traffic was involved. So I think we should know what we are talking about here.
In view of this I feel that if we were given some statement on national policy everyone would be happier. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred to this particular situation, which is of prime concern to the west, and I commend both him and the hon. member for Acadia for their speeches about free enterprise this afternoon. It is heart warming to hear these remarks, as one who comes from a city and a port which owes a great deal to one of our national transportation companies. I hope that these complimentary remarks, Mr. Chairman, will be taken as an indication that we are still interested in them, and we hope that they will be as interested in us in the future as they have been for years past.
In this regard the thought struck me that we were almost bordering upon the chief criticism which was made by the western

provinces, particularly Manitoba, during the committee hearings. I feel that, in spite of the minister trying to drag section 16 into the picture this is one of the major weaknesses of a big section of this bill. We are really considering maximum rate control philosophy. This is one fear the west has. I as a maritimer think that the government, if they are not already aware, should be made very much aware of the fact that, every day, the mari-times is going further behind, in this field of transportation.
The statements that have been made on behalf of private enterprise to the effect that the big bulk shippers should be allowed to negotiate with the railways and to set their own rates sound pretty good, but I go back to what was said in the committee hearings about the wastage of our resources in Canada. Let us take for example the potash industry, which is negotiating with the railways for special rates. In my humble opinion I think these rates could be set very high, and due to the monopoly or near monopoly situation in the industry, particularly in the international market, there will not be an accounting. In spite of all that has been said, the bulk shippers will not come forward and declare themselves; they will simply make up the cost of these high rates by taking it out on the economy in the western provinces, perhaps through labour or through some other means.
I leave with the minister these general observations on the bill. It is a question of watching these rates every day and in every way. Otherwise we will find that the difference in rates will be lost in the economy and that the western provinces will end up as we did in the maritimes. About 50 years from now they will wonder what has happened to them because they have no industry left and their standard of living will be well below the Canadian average.
So I say to my western friends, particularly in view of their appealing speeches on behalf of private enterprise, that while I agree with them in this philosophy they had better be careful of the maximum rate control section of the bill and not listen to the story which is put forward, that this is great and that we should let the big companies and the railways work it out themselves. That is my centennial warning for the new year to the western members: let them watch this section.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
I rise to speak on clause 1 of this bill, which will create a new national transportation policy for Canada. During our study of this measure in the committee on transport and communications I was interested in the area covered in clause 4, paragraphs
(a), (b), (c), (d) and (e), particularly in paragraph (c) which reads:
transport by water to which the Transport Act applies and all other transport by water to which the legislative authority ol the parliament of Canada extends.
I asked the minister in the committee why the seaway authority was not included or mentioned in the bill, and he gave me a satisfactory answer. Nevertheless I believe there is a matter which at present comes under the jurisdiction of the seaway authority but which should, I believe, come directly under the authority of the Department of Transport. I refer to the operation of the second old La-chine canal, which was transferred to the jurisdiction of the seaway authority when the seaway became operative in order that the free toll Lachine canal would not be a competitor for small ships. This canal has been partially closed. No through traffic can use it and only a small western section has been left open for local traffic. This means that very few ships use it.
However, whether this old Lachine canal carries heavy traffic, little traffic, or no traffic has no bearing on the difficulties encountered by vehicular traffic attempting to cross the 6th Avenue bridge between the cities of LaSalle and Lachine. In the course of the past ten years these two municipalities have time and again requested in letters and resolutions that the federal government build a new bridge, or an extra bridge, to solve the traffic problem caused by the present outdated horse and buggy federal bridge. Serious traffic jams occur at present when the canal is closed for winter. From time to time traffic jams extend from this bridge for almost a mile along two arteries to LaFleur street in LaSalle, westward on St. Joseph boulevard for 15 blocks and down 6th avenue to the heart of the main shopping street in Lachine, Notre Dame street.
This problem has existed for many years and each year it becomes increasingly serious. The seaway authority and the Department of
[The Chairman.]
Transport say that responsibility belongs to the municipalities and to the province concerned. The government has no policy with regard to the matter. I would point out however that during my lifetime the federal government has built two bridges over the St. Lawrence river. And as hon. members know, the Champlain bridge was completed only recently. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that a similar federal responsibility exists with regard to the building and modernization of bridges along the Lachine canal. It is my belief that the same degree of responsibility as the federal government assumes in connection with railway crossings should also be assumed with regard to bridge building across federal canals.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The first inhabitants of Lachine came in the year 1666, over 300 years ago. The first canal was built between the years 1821 and 1824, enlarged in the years 1843 to 1848, and again in the years 1877 to 1880. There was a complete reconstruction between 1896 and 1904. The four bridges which cross the two locks and the two water control systems were built between 1922 and 1924. They were built to accept the traffic of that era-the horse and buggy days. In the year 1904, when the reconstruction of the Lachine canal was completed, the population in the immediate area of La Salle and Lachine was around 6,000. At present the estimated population in the area of La Salle and Lachine is around 95,000. The serious traffic situation has been in existence for the past ten years, and therefore I believe that something should be done in this regard by the federal government.
I am aware of the possible closing of the Lachine canal. Personally I feel this canal, the first built in Canada, which enters the heart of the city of Montreal, should remain as an historic achievement. I believe it should be maintained as a harbour for pleasure craft and for Montrealers. The government has a policy for pleasure craft and I believe this canal should be part and parcel of that policy. There should be no more stalling one way or another in the matter of a decision. The Lachine canal should first be transferred from the seaway authority to the Department of Transport. Then a decision should be reached by the department or by the minister, either to close the Lachine canal and build a causeway between the two municipalities, or leave the canal open and build the bridge which has been requested by the two municipalities. I think the minister should study the possibility of creating a bridge fund,
January 9, 1967

in the same manner the grade crossing fund was created. I believe he should give additional power and responsibility in this regard to the new Canadian Transport Commission.
On December 20, when speaking in respect of clause 1, I addressed some remarks to the minister on the subject of railway crossings. I have an amendment which I should like the minister to study. I would hope that this amendment could be accepted by him:
That Bill C-231, an act to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions, be amended
(a)	by renumbering clause 78 on page 65 thereof as subclause (1) of clause 78, and
(b)	by adding, immediately after the renumbered subclause (1) of clause 78 thereof, the following:
(2) Section 265 of the Railway Act is amended by adding thereto immediately after subsection (9) thereof the following subsection:
(10) Where in the opinion of the commission any railway crossings of highways or highway crossings of railways at rail level, (in this section called a "level crossing") constitutes a present hazard to safety and no agreement satisfactory to the commission has been reached between the authorities or bodies concerned and the company for the construction of either such grade separation or such installation of signals as may be required for the removal of the hazard to safety, the commission shall
(a)	publish a statement, in at least one newspaper circulating in the area in which the level crossing is situated, of the action required to remove the hazard to safety at such level crossing, and
(b)	make a full report thereon to the governor m council for whatever action he may wish to take."
I should like the minister to study the possibility of accepting an amendment of this nature.

Mr. Chairman, at this point perhaps I might assure the hon. member who has just spoken that I will be very glad to give consideration to his amendment. I have come to the conclusion that the easiest way to deal with this problem would be to

I think in this way it would be much easier for hon. members of the committee to follow, rather than attempt to make two or three amendments by substituting words here and there. The amendment I would ask one of my colleagues to propose, if it meets with the general approval of the committee, I think would incorporate the substance of what hon. gentlemen opposite had in mind in respect of the three points. The new clause would be as follows:
1. It is hereby declared that an economic, efficient and adequate transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest total cost is essential to protect the interests of the users of transportation and to maintain the economic well-being and growth of Canada, and that these objectives are most likely to be achieved when all modes of transport are able to compete under conditions ensuring that having due regard to national policy and to legal and constitutional requirements

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to say a few words at this time regarding this bill in respect of a transportation policy in this country. Surely nothing more important has come before parliament in the past or will come before it in the future than this question of which the committee is now seized. We on this side of the house consider a transportation policy as a national policy. It has been the historic stand of the opposition over the years that a transportation policy is of prime importance. This attitude has developed from the concept expressed by Sir John A. Macdonald and his ministry, which brought about the unity of the provinces in this nation from coast to coast. Although in this year we are faced with a much more complex situation than existed in the past we still have substantially the same challenge before us which faced those pioneers who tried to build a great nation north of the 49th parallel.
It was particularly interesting to me to listen to the lip service given to the benefits which might accrue from competition, but those benefits cannot be used to gloss over the fact that for many years in many places the transportation services now in existence or likely to emerge will represent little more than a monopoly to the people in industry in those areas. A domestic air policy for light aircraft is one of compelling and vital importance today. This is worthy of more consideration than parliament has given it in the past. It is also worthy of consideration from the standpoint of the ultimate development of the manufacture of light aircraft in Canada.
When I listened to the compliments extended to the Minister of Transport I could not help but remember the stand he has taken in a personal way and as a front bench representative regarding suggestions brought forward in years past for the development of this nation. I make reference to this fact because I believe those who will be responsible for administering this act must in the future be concerned with this integral part of national policy. Great areas of this country must be
January 9, 1967

developed, and it is useful to establish guiding principles for those who must administer this act. We must give them direction in the establishment of incentives which will encourage that development and raise the standard of living to a level which will attract to this country the new people so vitally necessary at this time in our history.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I cannot help but think of the Pine Point railway and the attitude taken by hon. members who now serve in this government, and particularly the minister when he sat on this side of the house, as the government of that time sought to lay the foundations for a development that had not taken place in the past. I can only hope that when this bill is passed, its final terms will be such as to encourage development in those many areas of Canada that still require development, and may require it for a number of years in the future.
I think of the potash development in the province of Saskatchewan. I believe that the railways today are in a position to take care of that development. But when I think of the potential iron ore developments in the northern part of the province of Saskatchewan, I cannot help but think of the need for transportation in this regard. This also applies to the other minerals that we believe exist-and there is evidence that they do exist-in those northern areas. There will have to be much more of a pioneering spirit on the part of our railways and other transportation facilities than we have had in the past if this development is to proceed in an orderly and worthwhile way, in keeping with the concepts of this modern day and age.
Looking at transportation policy for Canada, I believe we cannot fail to give consideration to the potential posed by the Hudson Bay system, which generally speaking has been stalemated or at a standstill for so many years. In this connection I believe the provinces as well as the federal government will have to provide some incentives. Perhaps this is the time to suggest it, but I believe some of the provinces will have to provide assistance for warehousing facilities in order that there will be a two-way trade over those routes. This is one solution that might change the picture in some regard.
A while ago in this debate the minister referred to the vision. He did not really make the usual references that he makes when he talks about the vision, as it has been promoted from this side of the house. I believe that those who are responsible for transportation
Transportation
policy in this country must have a great deal of vision if we are to reach the development that our country deserves, and can achieve if we will it so.
If this bill can remove the discrimination that has existed between one portion of the country and another, and one station and another, sometimes within the same province or between neighbouring provinces, it will have removed some of the conditions that in years gone by have subjected our transportation systems to a great deal of criticism. The more I think of the references to competition in this field, the more I think of the railway systems in this country. As I see the situation, they have almost entirely failed-I refer not only to the national railway system but to the other railway system-to live up to the problems associated with those areas of our country which have a great potential for development. I emphasize and repeat that this is one of the cornerstones of a sound transportation policy as part of the national policy of this country.
That of course raises the whole problem of whether there can or should be subsidies to the transportation facilities that are provided, whether they are of rail, air or ocean. Looking back at the history of this country and considering our geography and the undeveloped areas that we still have, I cannot see how in 1967 and in the decade or two ahead we can proceed with the implementation of a national transportation policy that will not have somewhere within its structure those subsidies necessary to provide an equal opportunity to people in all sections of our country, and at the same time provide for the development of those areas that are so vital to the future if this nation is to achieve its real potential.
There will be other opportunities to deal with clauses of the bill as they come forward. I do not intend to make any further remarks at this time in regard to the general objectives that I believe we should be trying to achieve under a national transportation policy. But before I close, Mr. Chairman, I cannot help but say a word or two about rail line abandonment and the alternatives that perhaps should be given consideration. I think people across this country, and even those in areas which may face a problem of rail line abandonment, realize that uneconomic lines cost something to those who ship products, as well as to the other taxpayers of this country. But let us consider the situation in western Canada, where the Crowsnest pass rates were

January 9, 1967
Transportation
almost, and I believe were, a part at confederation itself-I see the parliamentary secretary shaking his head. I have always understood that the Liberal party was first and foremost in holding forth and promoting the idea that the Crowsnest pass rates should always remain inviolate; that they were one of the guarantees to those who live on the prairies, and that they now form, if not a written part of the constitution, indeed one of the unwritten parts which are even more vital than those which have been written in words in our constitution.
When we think of the effects of rail line abandonment in the communities concerned, I hope it will not be forgotten that other modes of transportation should be assured to those people so they will not suffer the personal cost and loss of their rights under the Crowsnest pass rates as they were originally guaranteed to those who went to settle in western Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have had only a quick glance at the amendment but with respect to the part in which I was interested I think it will go a long way toward satisfying the request that the Maritime Transportation Commission put forward.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Many hon. members may think that it is not necessary to play on words like this, but as we said before supper, when the commission begins its work it will refer to the directions regarding its objectives which are contained in this clause, and this is extremely important. I think that where there is any conflict between the objectives of the new transportation bill and the national policy objectives, by which the Canadian government can deal with the disparities in the rates in different regions, this amendment will have gone a long way toward resolving this conflict. Also this applies not only to the maritime freight rates but it might apply also to the seaway tolls and the Crowsnest pass rates. So that the statement of the protection contained in the amendment regarding national policy will make those in the maritimes who are concerned a lot happier.
The part mentioned by the hon. member for Peace River is good, I think, and his action in bringing it forward is worthy of commendation. I think this should be noted. Also we should keep in mind the flexibility of the government which has gone this far with regard to the amendment. I like the new phrasing
[Mr. Nasserden.l
which allows for the trading of commodities between the different regions, with particular mention of the export trade which is of concern to the eastern parts of Canada. It seems to me, after a quick perusal, to fulfil the objectives that I at least had in mind.

speechtext:
I have a few remarks which I should like to address to the Minister of Transport on this occasion. They are of a rather general nature and cannot be dealt with under any particular clause of the bill and therefore perhaps should be considered as an over-all comment.
The minister has been very co-operative up to now. He has paid far more attention to the suggestions which have been put forward than have any other ministers charged with the responsibility of piloting a bill. I think this should be drawn to the attention of the house. However, even though he may be paying attention to those suggestions this does not necessarily mean that he intends to do anything about them. I hope he will give more consideration to the west than just to say that the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who comes from the west, seconds the bill. This seems to be all the consideration the minister gives to the western provinces.
The bill before us is very complicated and far reaching. This being the centennial year of Confederation, this bill will perhaps affect people a hundred years from now. I think that the majority of the members of this house are not fully aware of its ramifications. Neither is the minister himself nor the people in the department. I do not think that the extent to which the bill will affect the lives of people in the future is fully realized.
One thing certain is that those people who are protesting vociferously at present will be affected immediately. One of our greatest concerns in the west is the fact that in the past we have been the ones who have been burdened with the payment of the bill of any transportation policy of the government. Whenever the railways have come around to settling their disputes, regardless of whether it concerns wages or the payment of interest on the capitalization of any of their projects, because of the fact that we in the west are further away from the markets than other parts of Canada we have had to contribute a larger per capita share of the costs than have the other more populated regions of the country. policy under the bill does not contribute to the increase of industries in the west.
I can well remember the time when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was the premier of Saskatchewan. On many occasions he trotted out the old Prince Albert pulp mill deal. This was offered to the people at every election. This particular deal was offered as a political bribe and incentive to the people. We thought it was a very good idea, regardless of whether we accepted it or not. Even now the present premier of Saskatchewan has gone so far as to assign to a firm the responsibility of conducting a survey or study of the potentials in the northern area. I would suggest that the bill does not offer solutions. The premier of Saskatchewan will not be any happier on the day we pass the bill than he was on the day when he first commissioned that survey, because nothing in the bill will lead anybody to think that there is a possibility of cheaper transportation. We already have legislation which is supposed to help the needy areas which the government is going out of its way to assist. And yet nothing is being done about the legislation which we suggest to the people is necessary to overcome the weaknesses in our economy.
When I suggest that transportation is one of the great problems I am referring to the fact that it does not solve our unemployment. Part of the problem is that people are simply moving out of Saskatchewan. We have been trained that way ever since the days when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was the premier of that province. We simply left this area to go to places where employment was more available, namely in eastern Canada. If eastern Canada is to get the benefit of this legislation, then I suggest that somewhere along the line we have been misinformed. I am not suggesting that subsidies are necessarily the wrong solution. granted to the C.N.R. or the C.P.R. or any other transport facility.

Transportation
This is called a transport bill, but I am suggesting it is a railway bill and that is the way it should be labelled. We talk about air transport. One commission is to be established with jurisdiction over all modes of transport. However, what we are dealing with here really is railway needs. Nobody is concerned about Air Canada not making a profit. Nobody is talking about that. What we are talking about is how to get the railways out of the red. If this is a transport bill, as has been suggested, there has been no mention made of the need of this country for roads. There has been no mention of what the government intends to do about the roads-to-resources program. There has been no suggestion what the government intends to do about providing alternative transport in cases where railway lines are abandoned. Will they assist the provinces? Will they approach the provinces in a meeting and say: Look, we have not got a policy and we cannot interfere with provincial jurisdiction, but we know if this railway line is abandoned some other means of transportation will have to be found. Is the government doing that? They are doing nothing. This pulp mill to which I referred is not going to be served. This lumber, potash, fish, or whatever you may have to bring out of these areas that are still not developed, is not going to be moved by the provisions of this so-called transport bill. The bill does nothing for the development of this country.
All this bill does is to set up a commission which is to be judge and jury; it is to be a court of record, as they say. The commission will be charged with the responsibility of getting all the information, and from whom will they get it? They will get it from the railways. If the railways suggest a certain branch line should be abandoned, they will feed information to the transport commission. The transport commission will ask, does it sound right?
How can the commission really make a finding when nobody contests these things? Nobody will be in a position to really contest these cases. Will there be anybody with the authority to challenge the railways to give all the figures? The transport committee of this house has never been provided with full information.
As a member of parliament I thought we should do whatever is necessary, be sworn to secrecy if necessary, in order to get all the information before the committee so the committee could decide for itself the value of this
[Mr. Korchinski.l
transport policy. Instead of that, what happened? The committee was denied information. How can the committee suggest a policy for the government when even the government itself shies away from mentioning these facts in the house? I do not think I took any oath of secrecy here to the effect that I was not to divulge any information. If the government wishes that type of ceremony, then I suppose it could be arranged. Then, a committee could be set up and sworn to secrecy, and that committee could be provided with this type of information.
We know for example which branch lines will be subject to abandonment in the next few years, and we know which lines have been frozen. Why could not this committee be set up to challenge the right of the railways to abandon these lines? I do not know where the lines are. So far as I know, the railway lines in my area are not the subject of abandonment proceedings. I am afraid that one day, after this legislation is on the statute books, all uneconomic lines will disappear and all the people served by those lines will be asked to move out. Why will this be done? It will be done because someone in the higher echelons of government, if you like, will have suggested that Saskatchewan is the wrong place in which to live. Suggestions have been made in the past that the people should move out of the maritimes.
This is not the right approach to a transportation policy for Canada. Let us face it, this is not a transportation policy for western Canada nor is it a transportation policy for eastern Canada. This may be a transportation policy for the people of Toronto. I have not heard too much objection from the Toronto area. This policy may be ideal for them, because they are right on the waterfront and have ships coming in to move their goods. Who is going to pay for all the combines that may be going out? There is only one person who is going to pay for them, and that is the westerner. Why must they be transported into one area, and then transported back?
Then there is the question of what is going to be done about the Crowsnest pass agreement. Never before has there been a suggestion contained in legislation that we study the Crowsnest pass agreement. We all remember that in 1961 there were rail lines that did not pay for themselves, and the minister knows it. These lines did not pay for themselves for several years because trade was being held back. What happened? The railways could very easily prove that they were losing

Then everybody has to struggle, without any assistance from the government, to fight the government transportation commission. The railway representatives came before parliament and told parliament to get this transportation bill through. They said the workers were demanding higher wages, and the railways could not pay them. Of course they were; that is common practice nowadays. After all, every other union is doing the same thing. Perhaps these higher wages were deserved; I am not trying to compare one union with another. But the fact is that the railways told parliament to get this bill passed because the legislation was preventing them from dealing with their workers.
That is nonsense, Mr. Chairman. I listened to what the president of the C.N.R. had to say and he impressed upon us exactly what was necessary. This bill will not do anything for the province of Saskatchewan. I wish the premier of that province had made the presentation of that province before the committee, but unfortunately he was away somewhere else in the beautiful Beechcraft plane he uses for his personal use. Had he appeared before the committee he could have told us how necessary it was to have a new air lines policy, or whatever is necessary.
You would have thought the province would have protested against this bill, because they are unable to put their pulp mill in Prince Albert into service. The bill offers no assistance in this regard. The government of Saskatchewan are in the same position as the former government of the province; they are unable to shift for themselves or to take advantage of companies willing to put up money. We talk of investment in Canada, Mr. Chairman, but Saskatchewan is just waiting for investment of this sort.
The minister is quit familiar with the port of Churchill, but we do not make sufficient use of the railway which was built to that port. For years the port has been shunned. Now that a few facilities have been built at that port the government are still able to find excuses for not using it to full capacity and for shipping out of Hudson Bay. Here we have a small town, every resident of which is willing to do everything in his power to attract industry. Yet they are struggling and are hoping that the province of Saskatchewan, the federal government and the railways will take them seriously. These are serious minded people and they want the railways to carry shipments from the prairies to that port. They have two mills operating there, but apparently the railways do not want their business. The government tells the people of Churchill that they are situated in the wrong area. It admits it is one of the have-not areas and that a little assistance is required, but they get it in dribbles. The government knows they are there if needed.
I have made mention of the lumber industry, but also in this area are silicon deposits which could be utilized by the mining industry. If the government would provide some assistance we would be able to develop industry in this area. Yet what does this bill do? It makes darned sure that the railway gets their share, and industry is told that if it is in the right place at the right time and shines up in the right way it will get some consideration also.

Mr. Chairman, it is with disappointment that I speak tonight on this transportation bill, because I wish the minister had accepted the sincere invitation I extended to him some months ago to take a trip east to find out how the people in my area are served with transporation. Had he done so I am sure that tonight he might have been able to provide some favourable answers to meet the problems we have been facing over a period of years.
It is probably repetitious to say that this long awaited legislation is welcome. For a number of years there has been much confusion in the transportation policies of this country, in the sense that there has been a multiplication of work in the absence of any clear direction our transportation policy should follow. Often additional expense was caused, not to the government but to the one who always pays, the consumer.
I realize that this legislation will bring under one board the matter of transportation policy and the provision of assistance to transportation in Canada. I am sure that the amendment which has just been moved by the Minister of Veterans Affairs will reflect the principles which should be inherent in a national transportation policy. I also hope it will serve to satisfy all regions of the economy which depend on transportation, and more importantly will recognize the regional problems of transportation.
I am sure that were we all to live within the golden mile of Canada we would not have too many transportation problems; that there would be sufficient room for all to operate; that competition would be good and that there would also be a satisfactory cost factor as far as the consuming public were concerned. This has been impossible. We shall never have a
[Mr. Korchinski.l
good national transportation policy unless we take into account those regional problems evident throughout the country.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I heard the hon. member for Mackenzie appealing strongly to the minister for ways and means to be found to increase productivity in the hon. member's province. The hon. member worried also about the increase of population in his province. The problems of our region are similar. Instead of worrying about the increase in population, our people are concerned with being able to live at the same standard as is enjoyed by people in other areas of this land. I am not denigrating this government in particular, but it seems that most governments forget the regional problems of the country. We are preoccupied with urban areas, with highly industrialized areas, and we forget about those hundreds of thousands of people living in the remote areas of this country-those people not living in the heavily populated, industrialized areas.
It is unfortunate that in 1967, in this country, we still have those problems which have been caused by the lack of cohesion between departments of government. There is no cooperation between departments. One department does not understand the problems of another. Although deputy ministers of different departments consult one another, making themselves aware of problems in other departments, it seems evident that what they do is not enough. For example, I can suggest a recent development in the department of the Postmaster General. I am sure the Minister of Transport is not aware of it. This development will deprive the Canadian National of much revenue, having to do with deliveries of mail to various parts of Canada. The mail, with this development, will be delivered a few hours earlier in most parts than is possible now. Had the Postmaster General's department and the Department of Transport consulted one another I am sure that the Canadian National would have found ways and means of delivering mail with the same speed as it is anticipated the mail will be delivered following the development in the department of the Postmaster General. Instead, what happens? We deprive the Canadian National of revenue and we pay out of the federal treasury more money for the transportation of mail.
We waste the Canadian taxpayers' money because we have not taken the time to understand problems, to try to work out some way to provide the service envisaged and save
January 9, 1967

untold dollars. We cannot deprive the Canadian National of all its income and then expect it to give that service we claim from it. This is one instance where we have been small, where we have been negligent. The Prime Minister said that we have looked after the social justice measures in this country. From now on I hope we shall look after those living outside the large areas, those living in the remote areas, and that they also will be considered part of our affluent society.
I can show the minister another instance where possibly we have been negligent with our taxpayers' money. I think of wharf construction, where we have built wharfs which to this date will never be of benefit to the people of this country. We have subsidized their construction, but those subsidies do not help consumers and do not reduce the prices of products brought to their homes.
For this reason I ask that instead of a committee of the house supervising the policy of the Department of Transport we make use of one of our ministers without portfolio. He could co-ordinate the activities of various departments. Such a minister could go into the problems existing between any two departments of government. He could bring his knowledge to bear for the benefit of our Canadian public.
I can also think of the policy this government has of meddling in provincial affairs, of building highways in provinces where we have no business building highways, outside of the Trans-Canada agreement.

Mr. Chairman, I sincerely believe that everything I have said has dealt with transportation policy in this country. I have not gone outside the bill as presented. I am suggesting that there should be co-operation and co-ordination between departments to better the national transportation policy of this country.
Transportation
I am deeply concerned about the manufacturing industries of the remote areas of the country. As the minister knows, the costs of production of industries in remote areas are high when compared with urban costs of production. For the products of remote industries to be marketable and competitive, those products must be moved quickly and cheaply to the market. I am sure the minister is also aware that industries in the remote areas require secondary products to be brought in, to help in the manufacturing process.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
This all involves additional expense and it is my contention that if we do not enable all these areas to enjoy the form of transportation which will help make their products competitive, then our national transportation policy has failed. There will be no prosperous Canada until these regional problems are solved. I think now in terms of air transportation, and I ask the minister whether he will consider the request which was made by the chamber of commerce in the town of Gaspe to extend the length of the present airfield there to 7,000 feet. As the minister knows, this area is far removed from the large population centres of eastern Canada, though the presence of a manufacturing industry, a mining industry and a paper industry in addition to the fishing industry makes it important that our people should have adequate means of travel at their disposal-a transportation system which would allow them to move fast and as often as desired. In order to make this possible it is necessary to provide airstrips which can operate in conjunction with a regional airfield. I hope action can be taken in this direction in the near future; I understand that some applications have been pending before the Air Transport Board for as long as a year and a half without decisions being reached. The people who are suffering most in this connection are those who are waiting. I hope a decision will be taken in the very near future to determine which carriers shall operate out of the region.
I am also disturbed about the fight continually taking place between the truckers of this country and the railways which operate trucking systems. It seems to me there is some ill will on both sides; I hope that they can make a pact which would prove beneficial to consumers, based on an arrangement whereby products will be brought into an area by rail and distributed by trucks. The piggyback system appears to be one which would help consumers in remote areas to get the benefit of

January 9. 1967
Transportation
cheap and efficient transportation. I cannot understand why the efforts of both sides could not be directed toward ensuring the cheapest form of transportation to those who live away from the more populous centres.
When I consider that in the lower St. Lawrence region 80 per cent of the products imported are brought in by rail, I also take account of the fact that in one large area some 150 square miles in extent, there is no railroad at all. The people who live in this area are obliged to pay an excessive price for transportation-as much as two or three dollars per unit for products which may cost only two dollars a unit. This is most unfair. Surely there is some means by which the national carrier could take the products as close as possible to the consumer, after which the truckers by land carriers, could distribute them. Surely some reasonable system of distribution could be worked out, even if it involved some subsidization.
Often in this house I have asked the minister questions in connection with railway passenger service, especially that between Ma-tapedia and Gaspe. I have invited the hon. gentleman to visit this area but he has not accepted my invitation. I have spoken to him about the cold buns. I have spoken to him about rail journeys lasting 24 hours without food. I have spoken to him about the toasters which he should have asked the C.N.R. to provide on their trains. Unfortunately I have not received an affirmative reply on any of these matters.
It is true the service has improved of late, but it still does not reach the standard which I think is appropriate. We have white table cloths, now, and we have serviettes of which we were deprived a year ago. When food is available, the quality is improved. However, people have recently been obliged to travel for 36 hours without having even a sandwich to eat. In this year 1967 it is ridiculous to ask people to stay on trains for 36 hours without even a cup of coffee or a sandwich to refresh them.
This happened on three or four occasions during the Christmas holidays. It was not the result of snowstorms. It was brought about directly through the negligence of the C.N.R., when it came to providing favourable service for 200,000 people. Even though the minister sits there laughing I hope he does not one day undertake that trip because I will see to it that he does not get a sandwich, and he will know what it feels like when he arrives at the other end. It is time we took notice of what is

going on in some of these other areas of Canada. These people have been patient. They have waited for years. The minister is still laughing, but the people of these areas where the service is so poor will realize that his policy will do nothing to satisfy them.
