Mr. Chairman, I think it is a matter of regret that the minister has seen fit to take an unorthodox approach in the drafting of this bill, or in incorporating in the bill a statement that really amounts to a judgment of its value. The wording of clause 1 of bill C-231 is not the kind which one normally would expect to find in the body proper of a piece of legislation. Clearly it is in the nature of a preamble, containing within itself all sorts of value judgments and premises which are highly questionable, and which have the effect of making the debate on clause 1 of this bill virtually open-ended.
Clause 1 refers to competition as the most salutary or most effective basis for a national transportation policy. That kind of assumption certainly is the kind which I for one challenge, and which a good many members on this side of the house, not only in this group but also in the group to my right, challenge. At least some of them have led me to that impression. I know that some hon. members have taken the opportunity to tell the minister that they agree philosophically with the premise that competition ought to be the basis for
Transportation
a national transportation policy, but other members have taken the position, much as I have, that the national economic needs are such that we ought to regard transportation services as more in the nature of a public utility. If one proceeds from that starting point, then he is led logically to the conclusion that we must continue to put considerable emphasis on regulation.
We really do not know what evidence the minister has which prompts him to postulate in the bill that competition shall be the effective basis of a new transportation policy. I certainly do not believe the minister would wish to get up and say he is convinced that today there is a possibility of sufficient price competition within the various transportation modes, such as would serve to protect the interests of the users of the transportation services. On an earlier occasion, before the Christmas recess, I took the time of the house to put my views on record, and I do not wish to abuse my privileges and rights here by repeating many of them. I do wish however to make some reference to the amendment to clause 1 which the minister offered this evening, copies of which were circulated to members on this side. In some respects I believe it can be said that the amending version is an improvement, but this is only in minor respects. In major respects there is a restating of the preambular wording or premise which I said was objectionable-that is, that an economic, efficient and adequate transportation system is most likely to be achieved when all modes of transport are able to compete under conditions ensuring certain things. And then the minister added the qualifier, "having due regard to national policy and to legal and constitutional requirements".
Were I in the position of the person drafting this legislation I would prefer, rather than use the words "able to compete", to rely on the words "co-ordination of transportation services" as being the most likely way in which to protect the interests of the users of transportation and the national interest. I really do not see why the minister should object to this suggested wording, because in clause 14 of the bill, which appears on page 6, the commission is charged with the responsibilities and functions of "co-ordinating and harmonizing the operations of all carriers engaged in transport by railways, water, aircraft, extra-provincial motor vehicle transport and commodity pipe lines". If the commission is to be so charged with the duty to co-ordinate and harmonize the various modes of

January 9, 1967
Transportation
transportation, then this would seem to show that we should postulate as the basis for a most desirable transportation policy that it should be based on the objective of having it co-ordinated and harmonized, rather than allow it to compete. We may not have been provided with sufficient evidence.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Let me say that the minister is being imprudent in relying upon competition as a basis for a good national transportation service in this country. His arguments in this regard are more of a barrage than based on reality. What are the realities in respect of competition in transportation systems in this country today? In large part I would say they are non-existent.
The amendment proposed by the minister to some extent accommodates the suggestion of the hon. member for Peace River who earlier today said that clause 1 should make provision for equalization of rates. The minister has been able to accommodate him on this point by the provisions of his amendment to clause 1 in paragraph (d) subparagraphs (i) and (ii). Paragraph (d) states:
each mode of transport so far as practicable carries traffic to or from any point in Canada under tolls and conditions that do not constitute-
Subparagraph (i) refers to an unfair disadvantage. That is one loophole. each mode of transport so far as practicable carries traffic to or from any point in Canada under tolls and conditions that do not constitute

When one takes all these things into consideration he finds there are provisions, stipulations, conditions and exceptions to any equalization of rates. maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC-DISCONTINUANCE OF MONTREAL-QUEBEC NIGHT TRAIN SERVICE
CANADIAN PACIFIC-DISCONTINUANCE OF MONTREAL-QUEBEC NIGHT TRAIN SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago, I asked the Minister of Transport whether he would agree to lend his good offices to the population of the heartland of Quebec and more particularly to the population of the riding I represent, to prevail upon the Canadian Pacific Railway to restore the night service which was in existence a few years ago when a train for Quebec left Montreal at midnight and when another train also departed from Quebec at midnight for Montreal.
A few years ago, the Canadian Pacific discontinued that service, claiming it was unprofitable. We do not admit this, because we say-and we are ready to prove it-that if the service was unprofitable, it is because the Canadian Pacific arranged for a few years to give such deficient service that it could not be profitable and passengers were kept away. First, the train was cumbersome and very slow; leaving Montreal at midnight, arrival was at three, half past three and sometimes four o'clock. That is surely prohibitive.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Pacific is obligated to serve the population, even if it is not profitable. But we deny that it is unprofitable and we are ready to prove it. Within the next few days, the municipal councils in my region, the Chambers of Commerce and all intermediate organizations interested in the economy of the Trois-Rivieres and the St. Maurice regions and the heartland of Quebec will redouble their efforts with the Board of Transport Commissioners and that is why we ask for the support of the Minister of Transport, in order that the Canadian Pacific may grant us this essential service once and for all.
The people in my riding are 85 miles away from Montreal and 85 miles away from Quebec city. It must be realized that we have to deal with Montreal and Quebec city firms. One also likes to remain in Montreal once in a while, to watch some sports event, a play, a recital or simply to spend the evening with friends or relatives, and the midnight train is very convenient for the return trip. It is the same thing for Quebec city.
Mr. Speaker, there is also one particular reason for making the request this year, and this is because of Expo, which will make for a very large increase in the number of travellers. If the Canadian Pacific Railways say they are operating at a loss, we will show

January 9, 1967
them that they themselves have already found a formula enabling them to make a profit. In fact, over the past few years, namely since this service has been discontinued, we have what we call a little train. In English, it is called "Rail Diesel train", and I believe its trademark is Budd. In French, it is called "le train autorail". This little train gets us home from Montreal in two hours. The personnel on board being very limited, it is quite economical. It could very easily be put into night operation to accommodate travellers from our area wishing to spend the evening in Montreal or Quebec city and those living in Montreal or Quebec city wishing to come and spend the evening in our area.
I repeat that we, our chambers of commerce and our municipal councils, are in a position to prove to the Canadian Pacific Railways that if they improved their service along these lines, they would make a profit. At any rate, even if it did operate at a loss, we feel this service should be restored for the duration of Expo.
Moreover, I repeat that our chambers of commerce and municipal councils have been making this request for years.
The hon. minister of trade and labour in the present Quebec provincial government, the Hon. Maurice Bellemare, made such a request himself, on numerous occasions, and so have a number of other public personalities in the area.
I ask the hon. minister, not only on my behalf, but on behalf of the municipal councils in my riding and my area, the chambers of commerce, the workers associations, on behalf of all the intermediate bodies concerned with the economy of the area, to support the request which will be made in a few weeks, and to make use of the considerable influence and persuasive powers which he usually displays when he decides to support a cause to be won.

IMMIGRATION-ADMISSION OF DEPUTY LEADER OF GERMAN NEO-NAZI PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked whether admission to Adolf Von Thadden, deputy leader of the neonazi National Democratic party of West Germany in his announced visit to Canada, would be refused on the same grounds that his American counterpart, Rockwell, is excluded from Canada.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I wish to make a distinction between nazis and Germans. I use the cliche that there are good and bad in every nationality and race. But there is no such thing as a good nazi. The National Democratic party of Germany is a neo-nazi party and in my opinion a neo-nazi is far worse than a nazi. The person who joined the nazi party in 1933 had no means of foreseeing the extremity of cruelty which that party would represent, but the neo-nazi, the nazi of today, knows precisely what extremity of cruelty was reached. Thus a man who joins the neo-nazi party today is, I say, far worse than the man who joined the nazi party in 1933.
Some people may say we cannot exclude Von Thadden because he is the deputy leader of a party, the National Democratic party. Well, the National Democratic party is not a political party; it is a criminal conspiracy. I am not speaking now about anti-semitism; there are simply not enough Jews left in Germany against whom anti-semitism could be practised. I have in mind one of the sadder aspects of the aftermath of the second world war-the fact that we speak always of the six million Jews who were executed. Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
11584	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Speaker, there were six million Catholics and Protestants who were also executed by the nazis in the crematoria-Poles, Czechoslovaks, Hungarians. I think we should keep in mind that those who died in Belsen and Auschwitz were people of other than one national group.
We do not allow people who are affiliated with Murder Incorporated to come to this country; yet compared with naziism Murder Incorporated is in a minor league. By allowing neo-nazis to come here we are giving stature to a party, to an ideology, against which the whole free world fought only 20 years ago. We did not admit Rockwell. It has been said we cannot refuse entry to Von Thadden because West Germany is a member of the O.E.C.D. and because Von Thadden is a citizen of a friendly country. Well, Rockwell is a citizen of the United States, a very friendly country which is also a member of the O.E.C.D.
The minister of the interior of West Germany-his name is Dr. Paul Luecke-has stated that the National Democratic party of West Germany is neo-nazi. I do not know what steps the security officers take in Canada to determine whether a person is acceptable here or not, but it would seem to me that one of the logical steps would be to get in touch with Dr. Luecke and find out more about the neo-nazi party and its background. There are more then one million Germans and people of German descent in Canada today, and there are also the survivors of some of these infamous concentration camps, and I would say that the overwhelming majority of these million Germans in Canada, and of these survivors, would be desperately opposed to the admission of Adolf Von Thadden into Canada. They ran away from the very thing this man is trying to reimpose in Germany.
In conclusion, I would say that the most vital area in the world today, the area which is virtually an armed camp, is the area where East Germany and West Germany meet, and that the ultra nationalism of this National Democratic party might very well set the stage for a third world war, possibly by storming the wall which separates east Berlin from west Berlin, or by a similar act of that kind. I believe Canada should go on record as being opposed to any neo-nazi movement and make it clear that a person who belongs to a neo-nazi movement is not welcome here.

NORTHERN AFFAIRS-"GRANDE HERMINE"- PERMANENT BERTH FOR REPLICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today in the absence of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development I addressed a question to the Prime Minister concerning a statement made in Quebec city on December 28 last before the Richelieu Club. The heading in Le Soleil of December 29 contains these words "La 'Grande Hermine' doit aller a Gaspe". This subject has been raised many times in this house on previous occasions. It has been raised because those of us who live in the Gaspe area take great pride in the fact that Canada was born in Gaspe on July 24, 1534 when Jacques Cartier planted there the cross in the name of the king of France. We are very proud of this and therefore do not like to see a distortion of history or historical fact. We are perturbed by the fact that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has stated there is a policy that the replica of Grande Hermine, which now rests at Expo '67, finally will have its berth at the Cartier Brebeuf park in Quebec city.
The controversy has been going on for many months. The two files which I have in front of me here contain extracts from newspapers. These files are voluminous, and the extracts all have regard to the same subject. I have yet to find an article which supports the suggestion that the Grande Hermine should go to the Cartier Brebeuf park in Quebec city. Mayor Jean Drapeau of Montreal mentioned that this is a national rather than municipal matter. He invited the mayor of Quebec city, Mr. Lamontagne, to come to Gaspe and tell1 the people of Gaspe that they could have the Grande Hermine because it is their right to have such a ship. The mayor of Montreal made an offer to the mayor of Quebec city that if they would give the Grande Hermine to Gaspe he would endeavour to see that another ship was given to Quebec. He said! that he would ask the municipal government.

to offer some guarantee that another ship would go to Quebec.
It is important to note that the mayor of Quebec city found the statement made by Mayor Drapeau very interesting, said that it deserved some substantial study and that he had an open mind on the subject. When Mayor Drapeau spoke I consider he was representing a population of 2 million people. In order to put on record the number of people in the province of Quebec who favour Gaspe as the final berthing for the Grande Hcrmine,
I should like to state the following. More than 500 municipalities in the province of Quebec have endorsed the petition of Gaspe in requesting that the Grande Hermine find its final berthing place at Gaspe-500 municipalities, plus the cities of Quebec, Asbestos, Chicoutimi, Charlesbourg, Granby, Hauterive, Joliette, Rimouski, Ville Saint-Michel, Verdun, Sept-lies, Lachute, Riviere-du-Loup, Matane, Port Cartier, Saint-Georges-de-Beauce, and Sorel. In this area there is a population of over 1,300,000 people, whereas there is a population of 2,500,000 people in Montreal.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
Among those who are in favour of berthing the Grande Hermine in Gaspe are the Lawrence Land Foundation for Historical Research at the University of McGill, many other historical societies and le chanoine, Lionel Groulx, and the curator of the Jacques Cartier Historical Museum at Saint-Malo in France. We have 15,000 signatures as well as many signatures of members of parliament who are in favour of Gaspe as the final resting place for this ship. There are 73 chambers of commerce in the province of Quebec also in favour of this site including the regional board of trade of Gaspe and the north shore, the board of trade of the Mauricie and the junior chamber of commerce of the city of Quebec. Among those also in favour of the Gaspe as the final resting site are the associations of hotel keepers of Gaspe and Bas-Saint-Laurent and the Press in the province of Quebec, notably Le Soleil, l'Action, La Presse, and the Montreal Star.
If the will of the majority is to be heard the government will have to reverse its decision in respect of the request of the people of Quebec for historical justice. By doing so it can help this economically depressed area to rebuild its tourist industry. I hope the final resting place of the Grande Hermine will be Gaspe.

According to Cartier's writings, the Grande Hermine was unable to cast anchor at Gaspe.
